Step 0. What and why

This step gives the business problem, the question for leadership and the method that answers it with historical data. Each later step answers one part of the question.

Purpose. This step answers: what must a new score do for the business, and how can we test it before a real launch? It supports this decision: approve a challenger cutoff for a champion/challenger test.

0a. The business problem

Situation. A lender gives unsecured personal loans with a term of 36 months. A risk grade puts each applicant in a sub-grade, from A1 (the lowest risk) to G5 (the highest risk). A lender approves the applicants with the best grades and declines the others. The public data does not give this rule. Thus we set the champion ourselves (Step 0b).

Complication. The business wants more approvals, but Risk does not accept a higher bad rate. Also, the 2015 loans lost money: the default rate went up and the price went down (Step 2e). A new score must also give reason codes for each decline and pass a model risk review.

Question. Can a new score approve more applicants at the bad rate of the champion, and does it add money?

Resolution. Build a challenger PD (probability of default) model with only the data from the application and the credit bureau. Train it on the 2013–2014 loans and test it on the 2015 loans. Then compare the challenger with the champion on the same 2015 applicants.

If the challenger wins on these loans, test it on 10% of real applications before a full rollout. The cutoff alone does not fix the loss of the 2015 loans. A pricing test must go with it (Part 2: Pricing).

Decision that this notebook supports. Approve the challenger cutoff for a champion/challenger test on 10% of applications.

Success metric. The approval rate at the same bad rate as the champion, and the realized NPV of the approved loans.

0b. Method and data strategy

A technical reader asks one question first. The champion declines some applicants, so where do the outcomes of these applicants come from?

The data has only the loans that Lending Club booked. It does not contain the applicants that Lending Club declined. Thus we cannot see the outcome of a real declined applicant. We solve this problem in three moves:

  1. Define a champion on booked loans. The champion approves the best sub-grades, up to about 85% of the 2015 applicants (assumption as-04). It declines the lowest sub-grades, about 15% of the applicants.
  2. Use the declined group as a test group. Lending Club booked the loans in the lowest sub-grades. Thus we know if each of these loans defaulted, and how much money it gave back.
  3. Compare the two policies on actual outcomes. The challenger approves the same number of applicants, but it puts them in a different order. Some champion declines become approvals (swap-in). Some champion approvals become declines (swap-out). We compare the actual default rate and the actual NPV of the two groups.

This method is a pseudo reject inference. Booked loans take the place of the declined applicants, so the method needs no model of the declined applicants. Each number in the comparison is an actual outcome, and a reviewer can check it.

The champion is our assumption, not the real policy of a lender. A reader must know this before any result. Each gain in this notebook is a gain against this champion.

Question Answer
What does a real lender have? A production approval policy. In a real project, that policy is the champion, and this section is not necessary.
What does the data not give? Lending Club published only the loans that it booked. It did not publish its approval rules or the applicants that it declined.
What do we build? Rank the 2015 applicants by sub-grade (A1 first). Approve the best sub-grades up to about 85% of the applicants (assumption as-04). Step 3c shows what this champion approves in 2015 and its bad rate.
Why this choice? The sub-grade is the real risk grade of a real lender, made on the day of the application. Thus the comparison is our score against an industry score. Only the cutoff of 85% is our choice. A fixed rule needs no training data, so Step 3 applies it only to the 2015 test loans.
Which assumptions go with it? as-04: the cutoff. as-05: the risk of the real declined applicants is not known. as-01 to as-03: the costs for the dollar values.
How can it be wrong? A real policy can approve more or fewer applicants. The real declined applicants are riskier than the lowest sub-grades in our data, so the swap-in result can be too good. A real policy can also use more data than the sub-grade, so it can be stronger than our champion.
How do we test it? Step 6d repeats the result for champions that approve 80%, 85% and 90% of applicants. The challenger must win against each of them. Step 7c proposes a small test below the cutoff to measure the real declined applicants.
What does not depend on it? The order of risk (branch 1): the scorecard has the same KS as the sub-grade, and we report this result as it is. The swap-set uses actual outcomes of booked loans, not estimates.
What does it mean for the claim? The notebook shows a method and the size of a probable gain. It does not promise a gain against the policy of a specific lender. The champion/challenger test of Step 7 measures the gain against the real policy.

Technical note. The comparison has these parts. Each later step gives the code.

  • Champion rule. The code gives each sub-grade a rank: A1 = 0 to G5 = 34. The cutoff is the rank of the 2015 applicant at the 85th percentile. The champion approves each applicant with a rank below the cutoff. A full sub-grade is in or out, so the real approval rate is a little below 85%.
  • Champion bad rate. The default rate of the 2015 loans that the champion approves. This rate is the risk limit for the challenger.
  • Challenger score. A scorecard (a logistic regression with WoE) gives the PD of each applicant from the application and the credit bureau data. A GBM is the benchmark (Step 4c). The grade, the sub-grade and the interest rate are not features, because they are outputs of the Lending Club policy (Step 2b). Step 5 moves the level of the PD to the recent default rate.
  • Approval at the same bad rate. The code sorts the 2015 applicants from the lowest PD. For each count of approvals, it calculates the bad rate of the approved loans. The largest count with a bad rate at or below the champion bad rate gives the approval rate. One scan of the sorted list gives the answer, so no search algorithm is necessary.
  • Swap-set at the same approval count. The challenger approves the same number of applicants as the champion. Thus the swap-in group and the swap-out group have the same size. The code compares their default rate and their realized NPV (Step 2e).
  • Selection bias. All loans passed the credit policy of Lending Club. Thus the result is valid only above that policy. A random test below the cutoff removes this limit.

0c. How the notebook answers the question

Each step answers one part of the question:

  • Step 1. Which data gives the actual outcome of each applicant, and what does it contain?
  • Step 2. Which loans, which target and which columns are fair to use? What did the current policy give?
  • Step 3. How do we test the score on a period that the model did not see? What does the champion approve on that period?
  • Step 4. Which columns and which model type put the applicants in the best order of risk?
  • Step 5. Is the PD at the correct level, and can the lender give a reason for each decline?
  • Step 6. Is the challenger better than the champion, in model metrics and in dollars?
  • Step 7. Where do we put the cutoff, and how do we test it with real applicants?
  • Part 2. What is the lifetime loss of each vintage? Does the price pay for the risk? Which charged-off loans give the most money back?

Business note. The question is a trade: more approvals at the same risk, with more money. The method compares the two policies only on actual outcomes, so each result is a fact of the past, not an estimate. Step 1 shows the data that gives these outcomes.

Step 1. Get data

Step 0 set the question and the method: compare two policies on the actual outcomes of booked loans. This step answers: which data gives these outcomes, and what does it contain?

Purpose. This step gets the data and its meaning. It supports this decision: if the data can answer the business question.

1a. Why this data

The data is the file of the loans that Lending Club accepted from 2007 to 2018. Source: Kaggle (wordsforthewise/lending-club), file accepted_2007_to_2018Q4.csv.gz. The data is a fair proxy for unsecured consumer credit, for four reasons:

  • The same product. Lending Club gave unsecured personal loans with a fixed term and a fixed rate. Many borrowers used the loan to pay their credit card debt.
  • The same data at the decision. Each loan has the application data and the credit bureau data from the day of the application. A bank uses the same data for its decision.
  • Actual outcomes and cash. Each loan has its final status and the total of its payments. Thus we can calculate the default and the NPV of each loan.
  • A public source. Each reader can get the same file and repeat each result.

The model uses the 36-month loans from 2013 to 2015. The data ends in March 2019, so each of these loans has a full outcome window of 36 months. Part 2 also uses the younger loans of 2016–2018.

The data cannot show three things:

What the data does not show Why it matters What the notebook does
Declined applicants We do not know the risk of the applicants that Lending Club declined. The pseudo reject inference of Step 0, and a test below the cutoff (Step 7).
Credit card behavior A card has a credit line and a balance that changes each month. A personal loan has a fixed payment. The method applies to cards, but with a different target and more data.
Macroeconomic variables The data has no unemployment rate and no interest rate of the market. The loans come from 2013–2018, a period without a US recession. The results do not show a downturn. The rollout plan uses guardrails and kill criteria.

1b. Key variables

The table gives the columns that the story uses most. The target is default. Step 2 makes it from loan_status. Appendix A gives the meaning and the use of all columns of the file.

Column Meaning in plain words Type Role
loan_status → default The final status of the loan. default = 1 for “Charged Off”, “Default” or “Late (31-120 days)”. default = 0 for “Fully Paid”. Text → 1/0 Target
grade, sub_grade The risk grade that Lending Club gave: A to G, and A1 to G5. Category with an order Policy: the champion rule. Not a feature.
int_rate The interest rate that Lending Club gave to the loan. Number (%) Policy and price. NPV and Part 2: Pricing. Not a feature.
fico The credit score of the applicant. Step 2 takes the middle of fico_range_low and fico_range_high. Number Candidate feature
dti Monthly debt payments, without the mortgage and the new loan, divided by the monthly income. Number (%) Candidate feature
annual_inc The annual income that the applicant gave. Number (\() | Candidate feature | | `revol_util` | The revolving balance divided by the revolving credit limit. | Number (%) | Candidate feature | | `loan_amnt` | The amount that the applicant asked for. | Number (\)) Candidate feature
emp_length The number of years in the current job, from “< 1 year” to “10+ years”. Step 2 makes it a number. Text → number Candidate feature
home_ownership Rent, own, mortgage or other. Category Candidate feature
purpose The reason for the loan, for example debt consolidation or credit card. Category Candidate feature
total_pymnt, recoveries, last_pymnt_d The total that the borrower paid, the money that came back after a charge-off, and the month of the last payment. Number ($), date Outcome: the NPV of each loan. Never a feature.

A candidate feature goes to the column selection of Step 4. A column with the role “Policy” or “Outcome” is never a feature. The lender does not know an outcome on the day of the application.

1c. Load the data and look at it

The code reads only the 36-month loans. It uses SQL (DuckDB) on the CSV file. The first run reads the full file one time and writes a small Parquet copy. Later runs read the copy in a few seconds.

The code reads two sets of columns:

  • The main columns for all 36-month loans of 2007–2018: the application data, the price, the status and the payments.
  • More credit bureau columns, only for the loans of 2013–2015. Only the column selection of Step 4 uses them.
Load: 36-month loans with SQL (DuckDB). The first run writes a Parquet file. Later runs read the Parquet file. 
# Purpose: Read the Lending Club file with SQL (DuckDB). Keep a Parquet copy for fast reloads.
# Input:   data/raw/accepted_2007_to_2018Q4.csv.gz, data/raw/LCDataDictionary.xlsx.
# Output:  `loans` (all 36-month loans), `extra` (more bureau columns, 2013–2015), `lc_dict` (definitions).

# 1. Columns for all 36-month loans. DuckDB reads them as text, then makes numbers.
COLS_NUMERIC = [
    "loan_amnt", "funded_amnt", "int_rate", "installment", "annual_inc", "dti",
    "delinq_2yrs", "fico_range_low", "fico_range_high", "inq_last_6mths",
    "mths_since_last_delinq", "open_acc", "pub_rec", "revol_bal", "revol_util",
    "total_acc", "mort_acc", "pub_rec_bankruptcies", "acc_open_past_24mths",
    "bc_util", "num_tl_op_past_12m", "mo_sin_old_rev_tl_op", "tot_cur_bal",
    "total_rev_hi_lim", "total_pymnt", "total_rec_prncp", "total_rec_int",
    "total_rec_late_fee", "recoveries", "collection_recovery_fee",
]
COLS_TEXT = [
    "id", "term", "grade", "sub_grade", "emp_length", "home_ownership",
    "verification_status", "issue_d", "loan_status", "purpose", "addr_state",
    "earliest_cr_line", "last_pymnt_d", "application_type",
]

# First run only: read the 393 MB CSV once and write a small Parquet file.
if not INTERIM_FILE.exists():
    INTERIM_FILE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    select_cols = ",\n  ".join(
        [f"TRY_CAST({c} AS DOUBLE) AS {c}" for c in COLS_NUMERIC]
        + COLS_TEXT
        + ["strptime(issue_d, '%b-%Y')::DATE AS issue_date"]
    )
    duckdb.sql(f"""
        COPY (
          SELECT {select_cols}
          FROM read_csv('{RAW_FILE.as_posix()}', header = true, all_varchar = true)
          WHERE trim(term) = '36 months'
        ) TO '{INTERIM_FILE.as_posix()}' (FORMAT parquet)
    """)

# Later runs: read the Parquet file (a few seconds).
loans = duckdb.sql(f"SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{INTERIM_FILE.as_posix()}')").df()
loans["issue_date"] = pd.to_datetime(loans["issue_date"])
# Credit bureau columns that only the selection funnel (dec-10) needs. Loans of 2013–2015 only.
EXTRA_NUMERIC = [
    "mths_since_last_record", "collections_12_mths_ex_med", "mths_since_last_major_derog", "acc_now_delinq",
    "tot_coll_amt", "open_acc_6m", "open_act_il", "open_il_12m", "open_il_24m", "mths_since_rcnt_il",
    "total_bal_il", "il_util", "open_rv_12m", "open_rv_24m", "max_bal_bc", "all_util", "inq_fi", "total_cu_tl",
    "inq_last_12m", "avg_cur_bal", "bc_open_to_buy", "chargeoff_within_12_mths", "delinq_amnt",
    "mo_sin_old_il_acct", "mo_sin_rcnt_rev_tl_op", "mo_sin_rcnt_tl", "mths_since_recent_bc",
    "mths_since_recent_bc_dlq", "mths_since_recent_inq", "mths_since_recent_revol_delinq",
    "num_accts_ever_120_pd", "num_actv_bc_tl", "num_actv_rev_tl", "num_bc_sats", "num_bc_tl", "num_il_tl",
    "num_op_rev_tl", "num_rev_accts", "num_rev_tl_bal_gt_0", "num_sats", "num_tl_120dpd_2m", "num_tl_30dpd",
    "num_tl_90g_dpd_24m", "pct_tl_nvr_dlq", "percent_bc_gt_75", "tax_liens", "tot_hi_cred_lim",
    "total_bal_ex_mort", "total_bc_limit", "total_il_high_credit_limit",
]
# 2. Same method for the extra bureau columns, loans of 2013–2015 only.
if not CAND_FILE.exists():
    select_extra = ",\n  ".join(["id"] + [f"TRY_CAST({c} AS DOUBLE) AS {c}" for c in EXTRA_NUMERIC])
    duckdb.sql(f"""
        COPY (
          SELECT {select_extra}
          FROM read_csv('{RAW_FILE.as_posix()}', header = true, all_varchar = true)
          WHERE trim(term) = '36 months'
            AND strptime(issue_d, '%b-%Y') BETWEEN DATE '2013-01-01' AND DATE '2015-12-01'
        ) TO '{CAND_FILE.as_posix()}' (FORMAT parquet)
    """)
extra = duckdb.sql(f"SELECT * FROM read_parquet('{CAND_FILE.as_posix()}')").df()

# 3. Lending Club data dictionary: one definition for each column.
lc_dict = pd.read_excel(DICT_FILE, sheet_name="LoanStats").dropna(subset=["LoanStatNew"])
lc_dict = (lc_dict.assign(column=lc_dict["LoanStatNew"].str.strip()

           .set_index("column")["Description"].str.strip())
print(f"36-month loans: {len(loans):,}. Extra bureau columns: {len(EXTRA_NUMERIC)} for {len(extra):,} loans "
      f"of 2013–2015. Columns in the data dictionary: {len(lc_dict)}.")

The data has 1,609,754 loans with a term of 36 months and 45 columns. Lending Club issued them from June 2007 to December 2018. The last payment in the data is in March 2019. The model years 2013–2015 have 546,165 loans. For these loans, the code also reads 50 more credit bureau columns.

The data dictionary of Lending Club defines 151 columns. Of the 2013–2015 loans, 82% pay other debt (debt consolidation or credit card). This share supports the use of the data as a proxy for consumer credit.

The status table shows the source of the target. Many recent loans are still “Current”, so they have no final outcome yet. Step 2 removes them from the scope of the model. The status “Does not meet the credit policy” marks loans outside the normal policy of Lending Club. Step 2 also removes them.

Business note. The data gives the actual outcome and the cash of each booked loan, with the data from the day of the application. It cannot show declined applicants, card behavior or a recession, and the notebook says where each limit matters. Step 2 selects the loans, the target and the columns that the model can use fairly.

Step 2. Clean and prepare data

Step 1 showed that the Lending Club file can answer the business question. It has the loans, the application data and the outcome of each loan. But the raw file also has rows that the model must not learn from. It also has columns that the lender cannot use on the day of the decision. This step answers: which rows, which columns and which values can the model use?

Purpose. This step makes sure that the data can answer the business question without bias or leakage. It supports this decision: the scope of the model, the target and the columns that the model can use.

The data preparation follows one tree with three levels. Each level has one split axis. Each axis divides all cases into groups that do not overlap and that together cover all cases (MECE).

Level Split axis Groups Section
Rows Is the record valid? If valid, is the loan in the business scope? Invalid · valid but out of scope · in scope 2a
Columns May the lender use the value on the day of the decision? If yes, does the column hold usable data? Not permitted · no usable data · candidate 2b
Values Why is a cell empty or extreme? Structural · operational · random missing values. Impossible · extreme but real values. 2c

Then Step 2d makes new features from the clean data, and Step 2e measures the baseline that the challenger must beat.

2a. Rows: which loans can the model learn from?

The first split asks if a record is technically valid. A record is not valid if it repeats a loan, if a key field is empty, or if an amount or a date is impossible. The code checks these four conditions. The code removes these rows before any other step.

Rows, level 1: technical checks, then the policy exceptions. Add the issue year and the target. 
# Purpose: Remove the rows that are not valid and the policy exceptions. Add `issue_year` and `default` (dec-01).
# Input:   `loans`.
# Output:  `loans` with `issue_year` and `default` (1 = default, 0 = no default). `row_checks` (table).

BAD_STATUS = ["Charged Off", "Default", "Late (31-120 days)"]
CLOSED_STATUS = ["Charged Off", "Default", "Fully Paid"]
DATA_END = pd.Timestamp("2019-03-01")  # Last month with payments in the file
n_loaded = len(loans)
N["n_loaded"] = f"{n_loaded:,}"

# Level 1: technical checks. Each check gives True for a row that is not valid.
row_checks = {
    "Duplicate loan id": loans["id"].duplicated(keep="first"),
    "Empty key field (id, issue date, amount, status)": loans[
        ["id", "issue_date", "loan_amnt", "loan_status"]].isna().any(axis=1),
    "Impossible amount (loan, funded amount or installment of $0 or less)": (
        loans[["loan_amnt", "funded_amnt", "installment"]] <= 0).any(axis=1),
    "Issue date after the end of the data": loans["issue_date"] > DATA_END,
}
invalid = pd.concat(row_checks, axis=1).any(axis=1)
# Level 2, first group: loans that Lending Club approved outside its credit policy.
exceptions = loans["loan_status"].str.startswith("Does not meet")
N.update({"n_invalid": f"{invalid.sum():,}", "n_exceptions": f"{exceptions.sum():,}"})
loans = loans[~invalid & ~exceptions].copy()
loans["issue_year"] = loans["issue_date"].dt.year
# Target: 1 if the final status is a default (see the glossary).
loans["default"] = loans["loan_status"].isin(BAD_STATUS).astype(int)
pd.Series({k: v.sum() for k, v in row_checks.items()}, name="Rows that fail the check").to_frame()
Rows that fail the check
Duplicate loan id 0
Empty key field (id, issue date, amount, status) 0
Impossible amount (loan, funded amount or installment of $0 or less) 0
Issue date after the end of the data 0

All 1,609,754 rows pass the four technical checks: 0 rows fail. The file from Lending Club is clean at the row level. The real work is the second split: which valid loans are in the business scope?

A valid loan can be out of scope for five reasons. Each reason is a different condition of the business question:

  • Policy. Lending Club approved 2,438 loans outside its credit policy (“Does not meet the credit policy”). The new policy will not make these exceptions, so the model must not learn from them.
  • Product. The question is about 36-month loans. Step 1 reads only the 36-month loans. A 60-month loan has a different risk, and a 60-month loan from 2015 has not ended at the end of the data.
  • Time. The model uses the loans issued from 2013 to 2015. For the 2012 loans, some credit bureau columns are mostly empty, because Lending Club added these columns during 2012. The decision below gives the numbers. The loans after 2015 have no full outcome window (see the decision below).
  • Applicant. Joint applications use a second applicant and other income and DTI columns. Lending Club started them in late 2015.
  • Outcome. A loan without a final status (“Current”, “In Grace Period”, “Late (16-30 days)”) has no outcome yet. The model cannot learn from it.

The outcome window. A 36-month loan needs 36 months to show its outcome. The last loan in scope has its issue date in December 2015. Its term ends in December 2018, and the data ends in March 2019. Thus each loan in scope had its full term to pay or to default.

Which loans give a default rate that we can trust?

Why this question matters. The PD sets the cutoff. If the default rate in the training data is too high, the cutoff declines good applicants. If it is too low, the lender approves too much risk.

Ways to do it. The problem is the loans that are not closed yet. There are only three things to do with a loan without an outcome: ignore it, wait for it, or model it.

  • Ignore it: use all closed loans of all years. This gives the most rows. The risk: a default closes a loan earlier than a full payment. Thus the closed loans of a young vintage contain too many defaults.
  • Wait for it: use only the vintages with a full outcome window. Each loan had 36 months to show its outcome, so the target has no bias. The cost: fewer rows, and the newest vintages are not in the model.
  • Model it: keep the open loans in a survival model. This uses all rows. But the cutoff needs one PD for a fixed period, and a survival model is harder to explain in a model risk review.

Evidence. The table gives, for each issue year, the share of loans with a final status and the default rate of the closed loans. The first method uses this default rate. If the method has no bias, the rate must stay near the same level across the years.

Evidence: default rate of the closed loans by issue year 
# Purpose: Show why a full outcome window is necessary (dec-01).
# Input:   `loans`.
# Output:  Table `dec01`: loans, share closed and default rate of the closed loans by issue year.

indiv = loans[loans["application_type"] == "Individual"]
by_year = indiv.groupby("issue_year")
# The first method uses only the closed loans. Young vintages have few closed loans.
closed = indiv[indiv["loan_status"].isin(CLOSED_STATUS)]
dec01 = pd.DataFrame({
    "Loans": by_year.size(),
    "Share closed": by_year["loan_status"].apply(lambda s: s.isin(CLOSED_STATUS).mean()),
    "Default rate of closed loans": closed.groupby("issue_year")["default"].mean(),
}).loc[2012:2018]
# 2012: share of empty values in the credit bureau columns that Lending Club added during 2012.
miss_2012 = indiv.loc[indiv["issue_year"] == 2012, COLS_NUMERIC].isna().mean()
N.update({
    "miss_2012": f"{miss_2012.max():.0%}", "n_miss_2012": f"{(miss_2012 > 0.3).sum()}",
    "closed_16": f"{dec01.loc[2016, 'Share closed']:.0%}", "closed_17": f"{dec01.loc[2017, 'Share closed']:.0%}",
    "dr_closed_lo": f"{dec01.loc[2013:2015, 'Default rate of closed loans'].min():.0%}",
    "dr_closed_hi": f"{dec01.loc[2013:2015, 'Default rate of closed loans'].max():.0%}",
    "dr_closed_17": f"{dec01.loc[2017, 'Default rate of closed loans']:.0%}",
})
del indiv, closed
fmt(dec01, {"Loans": "{:,.0f}", "Share closed": "{:.0%}", "Default rate of closed loans": "{:.1%}"})
Loans Share closed Default rate of closed loans
issue_year
2012 43,470 100% 13.6%
2013 100,422 100% 12.3%
2014 162,570 100% 13.7%
2015 282,934 100% 14.9%
2016 318,277 72% 19.8%
2017 296,484 41% 19.8%
2018 304,292 12% 12.6%

Decision. Wait for the outcome: the PD model uses the 36-month loans from 2013 to 2015, each with a full outcome window. The loss forecast in Part 2 models the open loans with a survival method (Kaplan-Meier).

Why. For 2013–2015, almost all loans have a final status, and the default rate of the closed loans stays between 12% and 15%. For 2016 and 2017, only 72% and 41% of the loans have a final status. The default rate of the closed 2017 loans jumps to 20%, because the defaults close first. A PD from these loans is too high, and the cutoff then declines too many good applicants.

The survival model is the right tool for the open loans. But the cutoff needs one PD for each applicant, so we use the survival model only in Part 2.

What would change the decision. If the business wants a cutoff for 60-month loans, it needs a separate model or the survival method.

The code applies the scope conditions in a fixed order. Each loan gets the first condition that removes it. Thus the groups do not overlap, and the table adds up to all loans.

Rows, level 2: keep the 36-month loans for individual applicants, 2013–2015, with a final status 
# Purpose: Keep the loans in the scope of the model (dec-01) and add the extra bureau columns.
# Input:   `loans`, `extra`.
# Output:  `df`: one row for each loan in scope. Table `row_tree`: the rows that each condition removes.

# Scope conditions after the technical checks and the policy exceptions (cell `clean`).
year_ok = loans["issue_year"].between(2013, 2015)
indiv_ok = loans["application_type"] == "Individual"
final_ok = loans["loan_status"].isin(BAD_STATUS + CLOSED_STATUS)
in_scope = year_ok & indiv_ok & final_ok

# Row tree: each row gets the first condition that removes it.
row_tree = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Not valid", "Fails a technical check", invalid.sum()),
    ("Valid, out of scope", "Policy exception", exceptions.sum()),
    ("Valid, out of scope", "Issue year not in 2013–2015", (~year_ok).sum()),
    ("Valid, out of scope", "Joint application", (year_ok & ~indiv_ok).sum()),
    ("Valid, out of scope", "No final status", (year_ok & indiv_ok & ~final_ok).sum()),
    ("In scope", "Loans for the model", in_scope.sum()),
], columns=["Group", "Reason", "Loans"]).set_index(["Group", "Reason"])
assert row_tree["Loans"].sum() == n_loaded, "The row tree must add up to all loaded loans."
row_tree["Share of loaded loans"] = row_tree["Loans"] / n_loaded

# Add the extra bureau columns. Each loan must match one row (one_to_one).
df = loans[in_scope].merge(extra, on="id", how="left", validate="one_to_one")
df.index = loans.index[in_scope]  # Keep the row labels of loans
# Check: almost all loans must find their extra columns.
assert df["num_sats"].notna().mean() > 0.99, "The extra bureau columns did not match the loans."
del extra  # Free memory
N.update({"bad_scope": f"{df['default'].mean():.1%}", "n_scope": f"{len(df):,}",
          "n_joint": f"{row_tree.loc[('Valid, out of scope', 'Joint application'), 'Loans']:,}",
          "n_open": f"{row_tree.loc[('Valid, out of scope', 'No final status'), 'Loans']:,}"})
fmt(row_tree, {"Loans": "{:,.0f}", "Share of loaded loans": "{:.1%}"})

Issue year not in 2013–2015 1,061,151 65.9%
Joint application 239 0.0%
No final status 86 0.0%

The model learns from 545,840 loans with a default rate of 14.1%. The time condition removes the most rows. The joint applications (239) and the loans without a final status (86) are small groups.

2b. Columns: which fields may enter a model?

A column can be a feature only if two things are true. The lender has its value on the day of the decision, and the lender may use it. The tree below uses these two questions as the split axes. Each column gets the first rule that removes it, so the buckets do not overlap.

Bucket 1: not permitted. The column has data, but the lender must not use it for the decision.

  • Rule 3. Known only after the decision. Payments, recoveries, later credit bureau data, hardship and settlement data. These columns contain the outcome. A model with them shows a perfect test result and fails in production. This is leakage.
  • Rule 4. The decision of Lending Club. The grade, the sub-grade, the interest rate, the installment and the funded amount. Lending Club set them from its own score. The challenger must replace this decision, not copy it (see Step 4).
  • Rule 6. Fair lending risk. The state and the zip code can act as a proxy for a protected class. The job title is free text with the same risk.
  • Rule 5. Out of scope. Columns for the second applicant of a joint application.

Bucket 2: no usable data about the borrower. The lender may use the column, but it does not describe the risk of the borrower.

  • Rule 1. Not about the borrower. Identifiers, links, free text and process fields of Lending Club.
  • Rule 2. Constant in scope. The columns that select the loans (term, issue date, application type) have one value for all loans in scope.
  • Rule 8. Not collected in the training years. Lending Club added some columns in late 2015. More than 95% of their values are empty in 2013 or 2014, so the model cannot learn from them.

Bucket 3: no mathematical value. Rule 7 removes the raw columns that a better calculated column replaces (Step 2d). Step 4 adds three more rules of this bucket: weak, duplicate and unstable columns.

Rules 1–7: the columns that the model must not use 
# Purpose: Apply rules 1–7 of the selection funnel (dec-10). These rules use only the column name.
# Input:   `lc_dict` (all columns of the file), `df`.
# Output:  `funnel` (each column with its rule), `RULE_BUCKET`, `candidates`, `CALCULATED`, `ENGINEERED`, `CAT_ALL`.

# Rules 1–7: a list of column names for each rule. Rules 3 and 5 also use prefixes.
NAME_RULES = {
    "1. Not about the borrower": ["id", "member_id", "url", "desc", "title", "policy_code", "initial_list_status",
                                  "funded_amnt_inv", "disbursement_method"],
    "2. Scope column": ["term", "issue_d", "application_type"],
    "3. Known only after the issue date": [
        "loan_status", "pymnt_plan", "out_prncp", "out_prncp_inv", "total_pymnt", "total_pymnt_inv",
        "total_rec_prncp", "total_rec_int", "total_rec_late_fee", "recoveries", "collection_recovery_fee",
        "last_pymnt_d", "last_pymnt_amnt", "next_pymnt_d", "last_credit_pull_d", "last_fico_range_high",
        "last_fico_range_low", "deferral_term", "payment_plan_start_date",
        "orig_projected_additional_accrued_interest", "debt_settlement_flag", "debt_settlement_flag_date"],
    "4. Output of the Lending Club policy": ["grade", "sub_grade", "int_rate", "installment", "funded_amnt"],
    "5. Joint applications only": [],
    "6. Fair lending risk": ["addr_state", "zip_code", "emp_title"],
    "7. Replaced by a calculated column": ["fico_range_low", "fico_range_high", "emp_length", "earliest_cr_line"],
}
# The three buckets of the column tree. Rules 9–11 come in Step 4.
RULE_BUCKET = {
    "3. Known only after the issue date": "1. Not permitted",
    "4. Output of the Lending Club policy": "1. Not permitted",
    "6. Fair lending risk": "1. Not permitted",
    "5. Joint applications only": "1. Not permitted",
    "1. Not about the borrower": "2. No usable data",
    "2. Scope column": "2. No usable data",
    "8. Not collected in the training years": "2. No usable data",
    "7. Replaced by a calculated column": "3. No mathematical value",
    "9. Weak (IV < 0.01)": "3. No mathematical value",
    "10. Duplicate of a stronger column": "3. No mathematical value",
    "11. Unstable (PSI > 0.1)": "3. No mathematical value",
}
# Calculated features (Step 2d) and the raw columns that each one uses.
CALCULATED = {
    "fico": "fico_range_low, fico_range_high", "emp_years": "emp_length",
    "credit_hist_months": "earliest_cr_line, issue_d",
    "loan_to_income": "loan_amnt, annual_inc", "loan_to_rev_limit": "loan_amnt, total_rev_hi_lim",
    "new_acc_share": "acc_open_past_24mths, total_acc", "bal_to_limit": "tot_cur_bal, tot_hi_cred_lim",
}
ENGINEERED = ["loan_to_income", "loan_to_rev_limit", "new_acc_share", "bal_to_limit"]  # New ratios (Step 2d)
CAT_ALL = ["home_ownership", "verification_status", "purpose"]  # Categorical candidates


def name_rule(col):
    """The first rule (1–7) that removes the column, or None."""
    if col.startswith(("hardship_", "settlement_")):
        return "3. Known only after the issue date"
    if col.startswith("sec_app_") or col.endswith("_joint"):
        return "5. Joint applications only"
    return next((rule for rule, cols in NAME_RULES.items() if col in cols), None)


# One row for each column of the data dictionary, with its first rule.
funnel = pd.DataFrame({"column": lc_dict.index})
funnel["rule"] = funnel["column"].map(name_rule)
# The columns that no rule removes, plus the calculated features.
candidates = list(funnel.loc[funnel["rule"].isna(), "column"]) + list(CALCULATED)
missing_cols = [c for c in candidates if c not in df.columns and c not in CALCULATED]
# Check: the code must read each candidate column.
assert not missing_cols, f"Candidate columns not loaded: {missing_cols}"
N["n_dict"] = f"{len(funnel)}"
N["n_after_names"] = f"{len(candidates)}"

Rule 8 needs the data, not only the name. It removes a column if more than 95% of its values are empty in 2013 or in 2014. The rule uses only the training years and does not use the target.

Rule 8: columns that Lending Club did not collect in the training years 
# Purpose: Apply rule 8: remove the columns that are empty in the training years.
# Input:   `candidates`, `df` (2013–2014 only, no target).
# Output:  `CANDIDATES` (the columns that go to Step 4), `miss_by_year`, `not_collected`. Table by bucket.

# Threshold of rule 8.
MAX_MISSING = 0.95
num_candidates = [c for c in candidates if c not in CAT_ALL and c not in CALCULATED]
# Share of missing values for each column and each training year. No target.
miss_by_year = df.loc[df["issue_year"] <= 2014].groupby("issue_year")[num_candidates].agg(
    lambda s: s.isna().mean()).T
not_collected = list(miss_by_year.index[miss_by_year.max(axis=1) > MAX_MISSING])
funnel.loc[funnel["column"].isin(not_collected), "rule"] = "8. Not collected in the training years"
CANDIDATES = [c for c in candidates if c not in not_collected]
N.update({"n_not_collected": f"{len(not_collected)}", "n_candidates": f"{len(CANDIDATES)}",
          "n_engineered": f"{len(ENGINEERED)}", "n_calc": f"{len(CALCULATED)}",
          "n_raw_left": f"{len(CANDIDATES) - len(CALCULATED)}"})

# Table: the columns that each rule removes, grouped by bucket.
by_rule = funnel.dropna(subset=["rule"]).groupby("rule")["column"].agg(list)
col_tree = pd.DataFrame({
    "Bucket": [RULE_BUCKET[r] for r in by_rule.index],
    "Rule": by_rule.index,
    "Columns": by_rule.map(len).to_numpy(),
    "Examples": by_rule.map(lambda c: ", ".join(c[:4])).to_numpy(),
})
col_tree.loc[len(col_tree)] = ["Candidate for Step 4", f"Raw columns + {len(CALCULATED)} calculated",
                               len(CANDIDATES), ", ".join(CANDIDATES[:4])]
col_tree.sort_values(["Bucket", "Rule"]).set_index(["Bucket", "Rule"])

Bucket Rule
1. Not permitted 3. Known only after the issue date 39 collection_recovery_fee, last_credit_pull_d, l...
4. Output of the Lending Club policy 5 funded_amnt, grade, installment, int_rate
5. Joint applications only 16 annual_inc_joint, dti_joint, verification_stat...
6. Fair lending risk 3 addr_state, emp_title, zip_code
2. No usable data 1. Not about the borrower 9 desc, funded_amnt_inv, id, initial_list_status
2. Scope column 3 application_type, issue_d, term

Rules 1–7 keep 79 columns, with the 7 calculated columns of Step 2d. Rule 8 removes 14 more. Thus 65 columns go to the selection funnel in Step 4: 58 raw columns and 7 calculated columns.

2c. Values: missing values and outliers

The candidate columns can still have empty cells and extreme values. The split axis for an empty cell is the cause. Either the event did not occur (structural), or a process did not record a real value (operational). Or a rare error lost one value (random). For an extreme value, the axis is reality: the value is impossible, or it is extreme but real.

Values: share of missing values by type, and the checks for impossible values 
# Purpose: Classify the missing values of the candidates by cause, and count the impossible values.
# Input:   `df`, `not_collected`, `miss_by_year`.
# Output:  Table `missing_types`. Table `value_checks`. Numbers for the text.

# Missing values: examples of each cause, with the share for the loans in scope.
MISSING_TYPES = {
    "Structural: the event did not occur": ["mths_since_last_delinq", "mths_since_last_record",
                                            "mths_since_recent_revol_delinq", "mo_sin_old_il_acct", "bc_util"],
    "Operational: the process did not record the value": ["emp_length", "num_tl_120dpd_2m"],
    "Random: a few cells": ["revol_util", "pct_tl_nvr_dlq"],
}
missing_types = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Type": t, "Column": c, "Missing (2013–2015)": df[c].isna().mean(),
     "Missing 2013": df.loc[df["issue_year"] == 2013, c].isna().mean(),
     "Missing 2015": df.loc[df["issue_year"] == 2015, c].isna().mean()}
    for t, cols in MISSING_TYPES.items() for c in cols])
# Rule 8 columns are operational too. One summary row for them.
missing_types.loc[len(missing_types)] = [
    "Operational: the process did not record the value", f"{len(not_collected)} columns of rule 8",
    df[not_collected].isna().mean().mean(),
    df.loc[df["issue_year"] == 2013, not_collected].isna().mean().mean(),
    df.loc[df["issue_year"] == 2015, not_collected].isna().mean().mean()]
# Keep the order of the types: structural, operational, random.
missing_types["Type"] = pd.Categorical(missing_types["Type"], categories=list(MISSING_TYPES), ordered=True)
missing_types = missing_types.sort_values("Type", kind="stable")

# Impossible values: a check for each type of column. Each check counts the cells that fail.
value_checks = pd.Series({
    "Income of $0 or less": (df["annual_inc"] <= 0).sum(),
    "DTI below 0": (df["dti"] < 0).sum(),
    "FICO outside 300–850": (~df["fico_range_low"].between(300, 850)).sum(),
    "Negative balance or count": (df[["revol_bal", "tot_cur_bal", "open_acc", "total_acc"]] < 0).sum().sum(),
    "First credit line after the issue date": (
        pd.to_datetime(df["earliest_cr_line"], format="%b-%Y", errors="coerce") > df["issue_date"]).sum(),
}, name="Cells that fail the check")
N.update({
    "miss_delinq": f"{df['mths_since_last_delinq'].isna().mean():.0%}",
    "miss_emp_13": f"{df.loc[df['issue_year'] == 2013, 'emp_length'].isna().mean():.1%}",
    "miss_emp_15": f"{df.loc[df['issue_year'] == 2015, 'emp_length'].isna().mean():.1%}",
    "miss_120_13": f"{df.loc[df['issue_year'] == 2013, 'num_tl_120dpd_2m'].isna().mean():.1%}",
    "miss_120_15": f"{df.loc[df['issue_year'] == 2015, 'num_tl_120dpd_2m'].isna().mean():.1%}",
    "miss_revol": f"{df['revol_util'].isna().mean():.2%}",
    "n_impossible": f"{int(value_checks.sum()):,}",
    "inc_max": f"${df['annual_inc'].max() / 1e6:,.1f} million", "inc_p99": f"${df['annual_inc'].quantile(0.99):,.0f}",
    "util_max": f"{df['revol_util'].max():,.0f}%",
})
print(value_checks.to_string(), "\n")
fmt(missing_types.set_index(["Type", "Column"]),

What we do with each group:

Group Example in this data What we do
Structural missing value mths_since_last_delinq is empty for 50% of the loans: these borrowers never had a delinquency. Keep the empty cell. “Never” is information.
Operational missing value emp_length is empty for 5.0% (2013) to 6.7% (2015) of the loans. num_tl_120dpd_2m is empty for 0.2% in 2013 and 5.0% in 2015, so the process changed. Keep the empty cell as its own group. Rule 8 removes the columns that are almost empty in the training years.
Random missing value revol_util is empty for 0.05% of the loans. Keep the empty cell. The group is too small to change the model.
Impossible value The checks above find 0 cells, for example an income of $0 or less. If the check finds a value, set it to empty. In this data, no change is necessary.
Extreme but real value annual_inc goes up to $9.0 million. The 99th percentile is $250,000. revol_util goes up to 892% (a balance above the limit). Keep the value. Do not cap it.

Why the data needs no imputation and no cap. Both models in Step 4 use only the order of the values, and both give the empty cells their own group. Thus an extreme value only goes into the highest bin, and an empty cell keeps its own risk.

Technical note. The WoE encoder (Step 3) cuts each numeric feature into 10 bins at the deciles of the training data. An income of $9 million falls into the top bin, together with all incomes above the 90th percentile, so its size has no effect. Empty cells go into a separate “missing” bin with their own WoE. The GBM splits each feature at thresholds, so it also uses only the order of the values. At each split, it sends the empty cells to the side that gives the better fit.

An imputation with the median or a fixed value (for example 999) puts an empty cell into a bin with real values. The model then loses the information that the cell was empty. For mths_since_last_delinq, this information is the most important part. The loans with an empty cell have a different default rate from the loans with a recent delinquency. A cap at the 1st and 99th percentiles (winsorization) changes nothing for a model that uses ranks. Thus it adds a step without effect.

2d. Feature engineering

Feature engineering makes a better input from the raw columns. The split axis is the number of raw columns that a new feature uses: one column, or more than one. The table shows what this data needs in each group, and what it does not need.

Group Method In this data
One column: numbers Bins and WoE Step 3 (the WoE encoder) does this for each numeric feature. A log or square root change is not necessary, because the bins use ranks.
One column: dates A date becomes a duration earliest_cr_line becomes credit_hist_months: the months from the first credit line to the issue date.
One column: text categories A text becomes a number emp_length (“10+ years”, “< 1 year”) becomes emp_years (10, 0).
One column: categories Merge rare levels home_ownership “ANY” and “NONE” become “OTHER”. Both models use the other categories directly. Rule 6 does not let us replace zip_code or emp_title with their default rates.
One column: a range A range becomes one value fico_range_low and fico_range_high become fico, the middle of the range.
More than one column: ratios Divide one column by another Four new ratios, see below.
More than one column: differences Income minus the installment Not used. The installment is the decision of Lending Club (rule 4).
More than one column: flags For example DTI > 35% and a delinquency Not used. A flag loses information. The GBM benchmark (Step 4c) finds such combinations itself, and it adds less than 2 KS points to the scorecard.

The four new ratios use only data from the application and the credit bureau. None of them uses the interest rate or the installment, because these are the output of the champion.

Feature Formula Business meaning
loan_to_income loan_amnt / annual_inc Capacity: the size of the new loan against the income.
loan_to_rev_limit loan_amnt / total_rev_hi_lim The size of the new loan against the credit that other lenders gave.
new_acc_share acc_open_past_24mths / total_acc Credit appetite: the share of all accounts that the borrower opened in the last 24 months.
bal_to_limit tot_cur_bal / tot_hi_cred_lim Utilization: the share of all credit limits that the borrower uses.

If the column below the line is $0 or empty, the ratio is empty (a structural missing value). The new features go into the selection funnel of Step 4 with all other candidates. A new feature stays in the model only if it passes the same rules.

The code also gives each loan a time and an event. Step 7 and Part 2 use them:

  • Default. The event month is the month after the last payment.
  • Prepayment or full payment. The event month is the month of the last payment.
  • Open loan. The loan has no event. Its time stops at the date of the analysis.
Calculated features (fico, emp_years, credit_hist_months, four ratios), and the time and event of each loan 
# Purpose: Make the calculated features and give each loan a time and an event.
# Input:   `df`, `loans`.
# Output:  Calculated columns of `CALCULATED` in `df`. `vint`, `o19`, `observe()`, `hazards()`, `months_between()`.

# 1. One column: text to a number, a range to one value, a date to a duration.
emp_map = {"< 1 year": 0, "10+ years": 10}
emp_map.update({f"{i} year{'s' if i > 1 else ''}": i for i in range(1, 10)})
df["emp_years"] = df["emp_length"].map(emp_map)
# One FICO value: the middle of the range.
df["fico"] = (df["fico_range_low"] + df["fico_range_high"]) / 2
first_line = pd.to_datetime(df["earliest_cr_line"], format="%b-%Y", errors="coerce")
df["credit_hist_months"] = (
    (df["issue_date"].dt.year - first_line.dt.year) * 12
    + (df["issue_date"].dt.month - first_line.dt.month)
)
# Merge the rare categories.
df["home_ownership"] = df["home_ownership"].replace({"ANY": "OTHER", "NONE": "OTHER"})


# 2. More than one column: ratios. No division by $0: the ratio is then empty.
def ratio(top, bottom):
    """top / bottom, or NaN if bottom is 0, negative or empty."""
    return top.astype(float) / bottom.astype(float).where(bottom > 0)


df["loan_to_income"] = ratio(df["loan_amnt"], df["annual_inc"])
df["loan_to_rev_limit"] = ratio(df["loan_amnt"], df["total_rev_hi_lim"])
df["new_acc_share"] = ratio(df["acc_open_past_24mths"], df["total_acc"])
df["bal_to_limit"] = ratio(df["tot_cur_bal"], df["tot_hi_cred_lim"])
# Check: no infinite values in the calculated features.
assert np.isfinite(df[list(CALCULATED)].fillna(0).to_numpy()).all(), "A calculated feature has an infinite value."


def months_between(start, end):
    return (end.dt.year - start.dt.year) * 12 + (end.dt.month - start.dt.month)


# 3. Time and event of each loan, for all 36-month loans of 2013–2018.
VINT_COLS = ["issue_date", "issue_year", "grade", "loan_status", "last_pymnt_d"]
vint = loans.loc[loans["issue_year"].between(2013, 2018) & (loans["application_type"] == "Individual"),
                 VINT_COLS].copy()
mob_last = months_between(vint["issue_date"], pd.to_datetime(vint["last_pymnt_d"], format="%b-%Y")).fillna(0)
vint["is_default"] = vint["loan_status"].isin(BAD_STATUS)
vint["is_paid"] = vint["loan_status"] == "Fully Paid"
# Default: month after the last payment. Full payment: month of the last payment. Open: no event.
vint["event_month"] = np.where(vint["is_default"], mob_last + 1,
                               np.where(vint["is_paid"], mob_last.clip(lower=1), np.nan)).clip(max=36)


def observe(v, as_of):
    """The time and the event of each loan, with only the data up to the date of the analysis."""
    age = months_between(v["issue_date"], pd.Series(pd.Timestamp(as_of), index=v.index))
    seen = v["event_month"] <= age
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "time": np.where(seen, v["event_month"], age).clip(0, 36),
        "event": np.where(seen & v["is_default"], 1, np.where(seen & v["is_paid"], 2, 0)),
        "grade": v["grade"].to_numpy(), "vintage": v["issue_year"].to_numpy(),
    }, index=v.index)


def hazards(o):
    """Monthly hazard of default and of prepayment, for months on book 1 to 36."""
    t, ev = o["time"].to_numpy(), o["event"].to_numpy()
    months = np.arange(1, 37)
    at_risk = np.array([(t >= m).sum() for m in months])
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        h_def = np.array([((t == m) & (ev == 1)).sum() for m in months]) / at_risk
        h_pay = np.array([((t == m) & (ev == 2)).sum() for m in months]) / at_risk
    return pd.DataFrame({"at_risk": at_risk, "h_def": h_def, "h_pay": h_pay}, index=months).fillna(0)


# 4. The view of all loans with all data (March 2019).
o19 = observe(vint, DATA_END)  # All data up to the end (March 2019)
del loans, mob_last, first_line  # Free memory. The steps after this use df and vint.
calc_view = df[list(CALCULATED)].describe().T[["mean", "min", "50%", "max"]]
calc_view["Missing"] = df[list(CALCULATED)].isna().mean()
calc_view.index.name = "Calculated feature"
fmt(calc_view, {"mean": "{:,.2f}", "min": "{:,.2f}", "50%": "{:,.2f}", "max": "{:,.2f}", "Missing": "{:.2%}"})

2e. Baseline: what did the booked loans give to the lender?

The data is now clean. Before we build a model, we must know the result that the model must beat. Two later steps need a dollar value for each loan. The swap-set (Step 6) compares the loans that each policy approves. The cutoff (Step 7) adds up the NPV of the approved loans. This section calculates that value and shows the baseline.

The data gives the total payments, the date of the last payment and the recoveries of each loan. It does not give each monthly payment. The code makes the monthly cash flows with these rules (as-06):

  • The borrower pays the installment each month until the month of the last payment.
  • The borrower pays the rest of the total payments in the month of the last payment. For a loan that the borrower pays early, this is the prepayment.
  • The recoveries, minus the collection fee, come 12 months after the last payment.

The NPV uses three costs. The cost of funds is 3% for each year (as-01). The servicing cost is 1% of each payment (as-02). The acquisition cost is $300 for each loan (as-03).

Technical note. For a loan with installment I, last payment in month n, total borrower payments P (without recoveries) and monthly discount factor v = 1 / (1 + 0.03/12):

  • k = min(n, floor(P / I)) months with a full installment, and the rest R = P − k × I in month n.
  • NPV = (1 − 0.01) × [I × (1 − v^k) / (0.03/12) + R × v^n] + (recoveries − fee) × v^(n + 12) − funded amount − $300.

The NPV for each $1 (npv_rate) uses the same formula without the acquisition cost, divided by the funded amount.

NPV of each loan from its actual cash flows 
# Purpose: Calculate the realized NPV of each loan from its actual payments (as-01 to as-06).
# Input:   `df` (payments, recoveries, dates).
# Output:  Columns `npv` ($) and `npv_rate` (NPV for each $1, before the acquisition cost).

# Assumptions from the assumption register.
COST_OF_FUNDS = 0.03  # as-01, per year
SERVICING = 0.01      # as-02, share of each payment
ACQUISITION = 300     # as-03, $ for each new loan
RECOVERY_LAG = 12     # as-06, months from the last payment to the recovery


def loan_npv(X, cof=COST_OF_FUNDS, acq=ACQUISITION, serv=SERVICING):
    """NPV of each loan from its actual cash flows (as-06)."""
    # Monthly discount rate and discount factor.
    i = cof / 12
    v = 1 / (1 + i)
    # n = month of the last payment, counted from the issue date.
    last = pd.to_datetime(X["last_pymnt_d"], format="%b-%Y")
    n = months_between(X["issue_date"], last).fillna(0).clip(lower=0).to_numpy()
    # Borrower payments without the recoveries.
    paid = (X["total_pymnt"] - X["recoveries"]).to_numpy()
    inst = X["installment"].to_numpy()
    k = np.minimum(n, np.floor(paid / inst))  # Months with a full installment
    rest = paid - k * inst                    # Rest of the payments, in the month of the last payment
    # PV of k full installments, plus the rest in month n.
    pv_paid = inst * (1 - v ** k) / i + rest * v ** np.maximum(n, 1)
    # Recoveries minus the collection fee, 12 months after the last payment (as-06).
    net_rec = (X["recoveries"] - X["collection_recovery_fee"]).to_numpy()
    pv_rec = net_rec * v ** (n + RECOVERY_LAG)
    # NPV = PV of payments after servicing + PV of recoveries - amount lent - acquisition cost.
    return (1 - serv) * pv_paid + pv_rec - X["funded_amnt"].to_numpy() - acq


def npv_rate(X, cof=COST_OF_FUNDS):
    """NPV before the acquisition cost, for each $1 of the loan."""
    return loan_npv(X, cof=cof, acq=0) / X["funded_amnt"].to_numpy()


df["npv"] = loan_npv(df)
df["npv_rate"] = npv_rate(df)

The table gives the baseline by issue year: what the booked loans gave to the lender. It contains only booked loans, so it shows the result of the champion policy of Lending Club.

So what: the 2015 loans lost money. The default rate went up from 12.3% to 14.9%, and the mean interest rate went down from 13.4% to 11.3%. This is the complication of Step 0 in dollars.

Business note. The model learns from 545,840 clean loans and 65 candidate columns, with four new ratio features. The baseline is clear: the 2013–2014 loans gave a realized NPV of $71.7M, but the 2015 loans gave −$32.9M (−$116 for each loan). Thus the problem has two parts: which applicants to approve (Steps 3–7), and at which price (Part 2: Pricing). Step 3 now splits the data so that the test looks like the future.

Step 3. Split data

Step 2 gave a clean target and 65 candidate columns for the 2013–2015 loans. Before we build a model, we must agree on two things. What does “a good score” mean, and which loans give an honest test of it?

Purpose. This step separates the data that trains the model from the data that tests it. It supports this decision: approve the challenger score for the test, with a result that is near to the result in production.

Steps 3 to 7 use the same small set of tools: the metrics, the WoE encoder, the GBM settings and the policy rules. The code keeps them in the file case01_helpers.py, so that the story stays short. The appendix shows the full file. The next cell loads the tools and gives them the categorical columns and the seed.

# Input:   `CAT_ALL` (categorical columns, Step 2), `SEED`.
# Output:  The functions and constants of case01_helpers.py in the namespace of the notebook.

import chart_style as cs  # Chart style (deck style guide). A second import is safe.

from case01_helpers import *  # noqa: F401,F403

3a. What the test must measure

A model project has many metrics. A reader can ask: “Why these metrics, and why not others?” Thus we start from the question that each metric answers.

The tree below splits the risks of a new score in two groups. The first group is statistical: the score can fail on the order of applicants, on the level of the PD, or over time. The second group is business: the score can be correct but add no money, or add money but break a law. A score that passes all five branches is ready for a test. If a score fails a branch, the team must explain the risk before a test. These five branches cover each way that a score can fail in production, and each failure belongs to one branch only.

Branch Question that it answers Metric Rule in this notebook Where we use it
1. Order of risk Does the score put the risky applicants above the safe applicants? AUC, Gini, KS KS above the champion. A complex model (the GBM) replaces the scorecard only if it adds 2 KS points or more. 3b, 4b, 4c, 6a
2. Level Is the mean PD equal to the actual default rate? Mean PD against the actual default rate, for all loans and for each score decile A difference of less than 1 point after the recalibration 4d, 5a, 6b
3. Stability Do the applicants of the test period look like the applicants of the training period? PSI of the score and of each feature Less than 0.1: stable. 0.1 to 0.25: examine. More than 0.25: do not use. 3b, 4a, 6c
4. Business value Does the score approve more applicants or add NPV at the same risk? Approval at the champion bad rate, swap-set, NPV More approvals than the champion at the same bad rate 4b, 4c, 6d, 7
5. Explainability Can the lender give the true reasons for each decline? Reason codes for each declined applicant Three reasons with a plain-English meaning, for 95% or more of the declined applicants 4b, 4c, 5b, 6e

Branches 1 and 2 are different. A score can put applicants in the correct order but give a PD that is too low. The order sets which applicants pass the cutoff. The level sets the expected NPV. Thus the notebook checks both.

Technical note. How each metric works:

  • AUC. The probability that a random default gets a higher score than a random non-default. 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect.
  • Gini. 2 × AUC − 1. It has the same information as the AUC. Credit teams report it because 0 means “no power”.
  • KS. Sort the applicants by score. At each score, calculate the share of all defaults and the share of all non-defaults below that score. The KS is the largest difference between the two shares. Credit teams and model risk reviewers use the KS as a standard, because it shows the separation at the best single cutoff. A cutoff is the decision that this notebook supports.
  • PSI. Cut the score of the training data into ten bins of equal size. For each bin, compare the share of the training loans (e) with the share of the test loans (a). PSI = Σ (a − e) × ln(a / e). The thresholds 0.1 and 0.25 are the industry convention.
  • Approval at the champion bad rate. Sort the applicants from the lowest PD. Approve them one at a time. Stop before the bad rate of the approved loans goes above the champion bad rate.

3b. Which period tests the model?

Which split gives a test result that is near to production?

Why this question matters. The lender will use the score on applicants of next year, not on applicants of last year. If the test uses the wrong loans, the test result can look good, and the score then fails in production. The approval cutoff then approves too many defaults.

Ways to do it. The split axis is time: where are the test loans in time, compared with the training loans? There are four possible answers, and each split method belongs to one of them.

Group Method Advantage Main risk Status
Same period Random split (out-of-sample), for example 80/20, or k-fold cross-validation Simple. The two sets have the same mix of years and the same default rate. Temporal leakage: the training data contains loans of the test period. The test cannot show a change over time. Possible. Test it.
Earlier period Train on later loans, test on earlier loans None for this decision. The model uses the future to predict the past. Production never has this data. Screened out
Later period, one cut Out-of-time split: train on 2013–2014, test on 2015 Same condition as production: a model from past loans scores new applicants. It shows a change of the population and of the default rate. Fewer loans for the training. The test result is often lower. Possible. Test it.
Later period, many cuts Rolling time windows: train on 2013, test on 2014. Then train on 2013–2014, test on 2015. Shows how fast the score loses power. More work. The first window is short. Possible. Use it as a check.

Evidence. The code makes each split and trains the same model on each one. It uses a logistic regression with WoE on all 65 candidate columns, because this model is fast and the same for each split. For each test set, the code measures three branches of the framework:

  • Branch 1, order of risk: the AUC, the Gini and the KS.
  • Branch 2, level: the default rate of the training loans and of the test loans.
  • Branch 3, stability: the PSI of the score from the training loans to the test loans.
Evidence: random split, out-of-time split and a rolling window 
# Purpose: Compare a random split, an out-of-time split and a rolling window (dec-02).
# Input:   `df`, `CANDIDATES`.
# Output:  `train`, `test`, `y_test` (the out-of-time split), table `dec02`.

# Out-of-time split: the model never sees the 2015 loans in training.
train = df[df["issue_year"] <= 2014].copy()
test = df[df["issue_year"] == 2015].copy()
y_test = test["default"].to_numpy()
# The GBM codes the categories with the levels of the training data only.
configure(train=train)

# The three splits. Each one is (training loans, test loans).
splits = {
    "Random 80/20 (2013–2015 mixed)": train_test_split(df, test_size=0.2, random_state=SEED),
    "Rolling window: train 2013, test 2014": (df[df["issue_year"] == 2013], df[df["issue_year"] == 2014]),
    "Out-of-time: train 2013–2014, test 2015": (train, test),
}
rows = []
for name, (tr, te) in splits.items():
    m = fit_woe_lr(tr, CANDIDATES)
    p_tr, p_te = pd_woe_lr(m, tr), pd_woe_lr(m, te)
    rows.append({"Split": name, "Training loans": len(tr), "Test loans": len(te),
                 "Default rate, training": tr["default"].mean(), "Default rate, test": te["default"].mean(),
                 **score_metrics(te["default"], p_te), "PSI of the score": psi(p_tr, p_te)})
dec02 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Split")

rnd, oot = dec02.iloc[0], dec02.iloc[2]

    "psi_oot": f"{oot['PSI of the score']:.3f}",
