A smaller tolerance keeps more columns, and a larger tolerance removes more.
:::

```{python}
#| label: backward-elimination
#| code-summary: "Wrapper: backward elimination with permutation importance (train 2013, validate 2014)"

# Purpose: Remove the weakest columns in rounds, with the GBM, on the training years only (dec-10).
# Input:   `train`, `CANDIDATES`, `fit_gbm()`, `gbm_matrix()`.
# Output:  `WRAPPER_SET`, `be_path` (one row for each round), `be_round` (round in which each column leaves).

BE_DROP, BE_TOL, BE_SAMPLE = 0.25, 0.005, 50_000
fit_part = train[train["issue_year"] == 2013]
val_part = train[train["issue_year"] == 2014]
X_val_all = gbm_matrix(val_part, CANDIDATES)
y_val = val_part["default"].to_numpy()
# Fixed sample of 2014 loans for the permutation importance.
imp_idx = np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(len(val_part), BE_SAMPLE, replace=False)
perm_rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)


def permutation_importance(model, cols):
    """Drop of the AUC on the sample when the code shuffles each column."""
    Xs, ys = X_val_all[cols].iloc[imp_idx], y_val[imp_idx]
    base = roc_auc_score(ys, model.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1])
    out = {}
    for c in cols:
        Xp = Xs.copy()
        Xp[c] = perm_rng.permutation(Xp[c].to_numpy())
        out[c] = base - roc_auc_score(ys, model.predict_proba(Xp)[:, 1])
    return pd.Series(out).sort_values()


cols, path, be_round = list(CANDIDATES), [], {}
while True:
    model = fit_gbm(fit_part, cols)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val_all[cols])[:, 1])
    path.append({"Round": len(path), "Columns": len(cols), "Validation AUC (2014)": auc, "cols": list(cols)})
    # Stop: the AUC falls more than the tolerance below the AUC with all candidates.
    if auc < path[0]["Validation AUC (2014)"] - BE_TOL or len(cols) <= 5:
        break
    imp = permutation_importance(model, cols)
    drop = list(imp.index[:int(np.ceil(BE_DROP * len(cols)))])
    be_round.update({c: len(path) for c in drop})
    cols = [c for c in cols if c not in drop]

be_path = pd.DataFrame(path).set_index("Round")
# Result: the last set with an AUC above the limit.
ok_rounds = be_path[be_path["Validation AUC (2014)"] >= be_path["Validation AUC (2014)"].iloc[0] - BE_TOL]
best_round = ok_rounds.index.max()
WRAPPER_SET = be_path.loc[best_round, "cols"]
N.update({"n_wrapper": f"{len(WRAPPER_SET)}", "be_rounds": f"{len(be_path) - 1}",
          "be_auc0": f"{be_path['Validation AUC (2014)'].iloc[0]:.3f}",
          "be_auc_best": f"{be_path.loc[best_round, 'Validation AUC (2014)']:.3f}",
          "be_auc_last": f"{be_path['Validation AUC (2014)'].iloc[-1]:.3f}",
          "be_n_last": f"{be_path['Columns'].iloc[-1]}"})
fmt(be_path.drop(columns="cols"), {"Validation AUC (2014)": "{:.4f}"})
```

```{python}
#| label: backward-elimination-chart
#| code-summary: "Chart: validation AUC against the number of columns"

# Purpose: Show where the backward elimination stops.
# Input:   `be_path`, `best_round`, `BE_TOL`.
# Output:  Line chart.

import chart_style as cs
cs.setup()  # House style (safe to call again)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
x, y = be_path["Columns"], be_path["Validation AUC (2014)"]
ax.plot(x, y, "o-", color=cs.NAVY)
# The limit: AUC with all candidates minus the tolerance.
limit = y.iloc[0] - BE_TOL
ax.axhline(limit, color=cs.GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
cs.label_end(ax, x.max(), limit, "Stop limit", color=cs.GRAY, dy=-8)
# The selected set in blue.
ax.plot(x.loc[best_round], y.loc[best_round], "o", color=cs.BLUE, ms=10)
cs.label_end(ax, x.loc[best_round], y.loc[best_round], f"{x.loc[best_round]} columns", color=cs.BLUE,
             dy=10, bold=True)
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("Number of columns in the GBM (rounds go from left to right)")
ax.set_ylabel("AUC on the 2014 loans")
ax.set_title("Backward elimination: train on 2013, validate on 2014, remove 25% of the columns in each round",
             fontsize=9.5, color=cs.MUTED, fontweight="normal", loc="left")
cs.action_title(fig, f"{x.loc[best_round]} of {x.iloc[0]} columns keep the AUC within {BE_TOL} of all columns")
plt.show()
```

**How to read:** each point is one round of the backward elimination. The line goes from all candidates on the left to the smallest set on the right. The blue point is the last set above the dashed stop limit.

**So what:** the GBM loses almost nothing from `{python} N["n_all"]` to `{python} N["n_wrapper"]` columns. The validation AUC goes from `{python} N["be_auc0"]` to `{python} N["be_auc_best"]`. With fewer columns, the AUC falls fast (`{python} N["be_auc_last"]` with `{python} N["be_n_last"]` columns). Thus most of the candidates carry the same information.

**Evidence 3: the three sets on the 2015 test.** The code trains the same GBM on all 2013–2014 loans with each set of columns. It then scores the 2015 loans.

Three metrics compare the sets. The AUC measures the order of the applicants. The KS measures the best separation of defaults and non-defaults. The approval rate at the bad rate of the champion is the business test.

```{python}
#| label: selection-compare
#| code-summary: "Comparison on the 2015 test: filter, embedded (all candidates) and wrapper"

# Purpose: Compare the three selection methods with the same GBM on the 2015 loans (dec-10).
# Input:   `train`, `test`, `FUNNEL_SET`, `WRAPPER_SET`, `CANDIDATES`, `champ_bad`.
# Output:  `gbm_by_option` (model and PD on the test for each set), table `dec10`.

options = {"Filter: selection funnel": FUNNEL_SET, "Wrapper: backward elimination": WRAPPER_SET,
           "Embedded: GBM on all candidates": CANDIDATES}
fits, rows = {}, []
for name, cols in options.items():
    model = fit_gbm(train, cols)
    p = model.predict_proba(gbm_matrix(test, cols))[:, 1]
    fits[name] = (model, p)
    rows.append({"Method": name, "Features": len(cols), **score_metrics(test["default"], p),
                 "Approval at champion bad rate": approval_at_bad_rate(test["default"], p, champ_bad)})
dec10 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Method")
in_both = sorted(set(FUNNEL_SET) & set(WRAPPER_SET))
N.update({
    "auc_funnel": f"{dec10.iloc[0]['AUC']:.3f}", "auc_wrapper": f"{dec10.iloc[1]['AUC']:.3f}",
    "auc_all": f"{dec10.iloc[2]['AUC']:.3f}",
    "appr_funnel": f"{dec10.iloc[0]['Approval at champion bad rate']:.1%}",
    "appr_wrapper": f"{dec10.iloc[1]['Approval at champion bad rate']:.1%}",
    "appr_all": f"{dec10.iloc[2]['Approval at champion bad rate']:.1%}",
    "n_both": f"{len(in_both)}",
    "only_wrapper": ", ".join(f"`{c}`" for c in sorted(set(WRAPPER_SET) - set(FUNNEL_SET))) or "none",
})
fmt(dec10, {"AUC": "{:.3f}", "Gini": "{:.3f}", "KS": "{:.3f}", "Approval at champion bad rate": "{:.1%}"})
```

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** Use the columns of the selection funnel (the filter). Use the backward elimination as a check of the funnel.
:::

**Why.** The three methods give almost the same result on the 2015 loans. The AUC is `{python} N["auc_funnel"]` for the funnel, `{python} N["auc_wrapper"]` for the wrapper and `{python} N["auc_all"]` for all candidates. At the champion bad rate, they approve `{python} N["appr_funnel"]`, `{python} N["appr_wrapper"]` and `{python} N["appr_all"]` of the applicants. Thus more columns, or a search with the model, add almost no power.

When the methods give the same power, the reason for each column decides. The funnel gives each removed column a written rule, and [Appendix A](#data-dictionary) shows it for each column. The wrapper gives only "the model did not need it", and its set can change with the validation sample.

The two methods agree on `{python} N["n_both"]` columns. The wrapper also keeps these columns that the funnel removes: `{python} N["only_wrapper"]`. They can help a model in combination with other columns. But the wrapper set approves `{python} N["appr_wrapper"]` of the applicants, against `{python} N["appr_funnel"]` for the funnel.

**What would change the decision.** If the wrapper approves 1 point more applicants on a later vintage at the champion bad rate, use its set. Then write a reason for each of its columns.
:::

```{python}
#| label: funnel-table
#| code-summary: "Final features and the status of each column (one row for each column)"

# Purpose: Fix the final features. Give each column its bucket, rule and detail (dec-10, Appendix A).
# Input:   `funnel`, `FUNNEL_SET`, `weak`, `duplicate_of`, `unstable`, `fits`, `be_round`, `lc_dict`.
# Output:  `FEATURES`, `NUM_FEATURES`, `CAT_FEATURES`, `gbm_by_option`, `column_status`, table of the funnel.

FEATURES = list(FUNNEL_SET)
NUM_FEATURES, CAT_FEATURES = split_types(FEATURES)
# Step 4b and later use the key "B. Selection funnel" for the GBM on the final features.
gbm_by_option = {"B. Selection funnel": fits["Filter: selection funnel"],
                 "Backward elimination": fits["Wrapper: backward elimination"],
                 "All candidates": fits["Embedded: GBM on all candidates"]}

# Rules 9–11 and the features, for the columns of the file.
for cols, rule in [(weak, "9. Weak (IV < 0.01)"), (list(duplicate_of), "10. Duplicate of a stronger column"),
                   (unstable, "11. Unstable (PSI > 0.1)")]:
    funnel.loc[funnel["column"].isin(cols), "rule"] = rule
funnel.loc[funnel["column"].isin(FEATURES), "rule"] = "Feature"

# One row for each column of the file, then one row for each calculated feature.
REPLACED_BY = {raw: calc for calc, raws in CALCULATED.items() if calc in ("fico", "emp_years", "credit_hist_months")
               for raw in raws.split(", ") if raw != "issue_d"}
rule_of = funnel.set_index("column")["rule"].to_dict()
for c in CALCULATED:
    rule_of[c] = ("9. Weak (IV < 0.01)" if c in weak else "10. Duplicate of a stronger column" if c in duplicate_of
                  else "11. Unstable (PSI > 0.1)" if c in unstable else "Feature")


def status_detail(c):
    """Short text with the evidence for the status of one column."""
    rule = rule_of.get(c)
    if rule == "Feature" or (rule and rule.startswith("9.")):
        text = f"IV {iv_all[c]:.3f}"
    elif rule and rule.startswith("10."):
        text = f"Duplicate of {duplicate_of[c]} (IV {iv_all[c]:.3f})"
    elif rule and rule.startswith("11."):
        text = f"PSI {psi_col[c]:.2f}"
    elif rule and rule.startswith("8."):
        text = f"Missing up to {miss_by_year.loc[c].max():.0%} in 2013–2014"
    elif rule and rule.startswith("7."):
        text = f"Replaced by {REPLACED_BY[c]}"
    else:
        return ""
    if c in CANDIDATES:  # Result of the wrapper as a check
        text += "; wrapper keeps it" if c in WRAPPER_SET else f"; wrapper removes it in round {be_round[c]}"
    return text


column_status = pd.DataFrame({"column": list(lc_dict.index) + list(CALCULATED)})
column_status["rule"] = column_status["column"].map(rule_of).fillna("Candidate")
column_status["bucket"] = column_status["rule"].map(RULE_BUCKET).fillna(column_status["rule"])
column_status["detail"] = column_status["column"].map(status_detail)
column_status = column_status[["column", "bucket", "rule", "detail"]]
assert column_status["rule"].ne("Candidate").all(), "Each column must have a status."

N.update({"n_features": f"{len(FEATURES)}",
          # Same keys as the first version, for the text of later parts.
          "auc_b": N["auc_funnel"], "appr_b": N["appr_funnel"], "auc_c": N["auc_all"], "appr_c": N["appr_all"]})

# Table of the funnel: the columns that each rule removes, by bucket.
table = (column_status.groupby(["bucket", "rule"])["column"]
         .agg(Columns="size", Examples=lambda c: ", ".join(list(c)[:4])).reset_index())
# Order: buckets 1–3 with the rules by number, then the features.
table["_r"] = table["rule"].str.extract(r"^(\d+)\.")[0].astype(float).fillna(99)
table = (table.sort_values(["bucket", "_r"]).drop(columns="_r")
         .rename(columns={"bucket": "Bucket", "rule": "Rule"}).set_index(["Bucket", "Rule"]))
table
```

The funnel keeps `{python} N["n_features"]` columns as features. The table gives the IV of each feature on the training data.

```{python}
#| label: iv
#| code-summary: "Information value of each feature (training data)"

# Purpose: Show the IV of each final feature.
# Input:   `iv_all`, `FEATURES`, `ENGINEERED`.
# Output:  Table of IV values.

iv_table = iv_all.reindex(FEATURES).rename("IV").to_frame()
iv_table["Type"] = ["New ratio (Step 2d)" if c in ENGINEERED else "Calculated (Step 2d)" if c in CALCULATED
                    else "Raw column" for c in FEATURES]
fmt(iv_table, {"IV": "{:.3f}"})
```

## 4b. Lending Club sub-grade

Step 4a selected the columns from the application and the credit bureau. One strong column is not in the list: the Lending Club sub-grade. Rule 4 of Step 2 removed it, because it is the output of the Lending Club policy. This section examines if that rule costs too much power.

::: {#dec-03 .decision}
### Can the challenger use the Lending Club sub-grade? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The sub-grade is the score of the champion. If the challenger uses it, the challenger can be stronger, but it is then not a separate policy. A lender must also explain each decline, and nobody outside Lending Club can explain the sub-grade.

**Ways to do it.** The axis is the role of the sub-grade in the challenger. There are three roles, and they cover all cases: an input, no role, or a first stage.

| Role | What it is | Advantage | Main risk | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Input | The sub-grade is one feature of the challenger. | Higher AUC: the sub-grade contains data that we do not have. | Part of each decline comes from a model that we cannot see. No true reason code for that part. | Test it |
| No role | The challenger uses only the application and the credit bureau. The sub-grade is only the benchmark. | A true challenger. Each reason code comes from a feature that we can explain. | Lower AUC than the input role. | Test it |
| First stage | The champion decides first. The challenger then changes the decision only inside each grade (an overlay). | The reason codes of the champion stay. | It needs the champion in production. It is a different project. | Screened out here. See the last line of this block. |

**Evidence.** The code trains a logistic regression with WoE twice, with and without the sub-grade. It compares both with the champion on the 2015 loans. Each score approves the same share of applicants as the champion. The table shows branch 1 (order of risk) and branch 4 (bad rate of the approved loans). The swap-set column gives the share of applicants where the score and the champion do not agree.

```{python}
#| label: dec-03-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: champion, challenger with sub-grade, challenger without sub-grade"

# Purpose: Compare the champion with two challengers: with and without the sub-grade (dec-03).
# Input:   `train`, `test`, `FEATURES`, `champ_ok`.
# Output:  `m_lr`, `pd_test_lr` (PD of the logistic regression), table `dec03`.

# No role: logistic regression with WoE, without the sub-grade.
m_lr = fit_woe_lr(train, FEATURES)
pd_test_lr = pd_woe_lr(m_lr, test)

# Input: the same model, plus the sub-grade as a number (A1 = 0, G5 = 34).
train_g = train.assign(sub_grade_num=subgrade_rank(train))
test_g = test.assign(sub_grade_num=subgrade_rank(test))
m_lr_g = fit_woe_lr(train_g, FEATURES + ["sub_grade_num"])
pd_test_lr_g = pd_woe_lr(m_lr_g, test_g)

# Each score approves the same share as the champion. Compare the bad rate and the swap-set.
rows = []
for name, risk in [("Champion: sub-grade only", champ_rank + rng.random(len(champ_rank)) * 0.01),
                   ("Challenger, sub-grade as an input", pd_test_lr_g),
                   ("Challenger, no sub-grade", pd_test_lr)]:
    ok = approve_top(risk, champ_ok.mean())
    rows.append({"Score (logistic regression with WoE)": name,
                 **score_metrics(test["default"], risk),
                 "Swap-set": np.mean(ok != champ_ok),
                 "Bad rate of approved": test["default"].to_numpy()[ok].mean()})
dec03 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Score (logistic regression with WoE)")
N.update({"auc_with_sg": f"{dec03.iloc[1]['AUC']:.3f}", "auc_no_sg": f"{dec03.iloc[2]['AUC']:.3f}",
          "auc_champ": f"{dec03.iloc[0]['AUC']:.3f}"})
fmt(dec03, {"AUC": "{:.3f}", "Gini": "{:.3f}", "KS": "{:.3f}",
            "Swap-set": "{:.1%}", "Bad rate of approved": "{:.2%}"})
```

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** The challenger does not use the sub-grade. The sub-grade is only the benchmark.
:::

**Why.** With the sub-grade as an input, the AUC is `{python} N["auc_with_sg"]`, the highest of the three. But an adverse action notice must give the real reasons for a decline. With the sub-grade as an input, part of each decline comes from a source that we cannot explain (branch 5 fails).

Without the sub-grade, the logistic regression has an AUC of `{python} N["auc_no_sg"]`. The champion has `{python} N["auc_champ"]`. Thus a logistic regression on our features is at the level of the champion, without the score of Lending Club. Section 4c examines if a different model type finds more risk in the same features.

**What would change the decision.** If the champion stays in production and the challenger becomes an overlay on the champion score, use the first-stage role. The lender then has the reason codes of the champion.
:::

## 4c. Model type

Section 4b showed that a logistic regression with WoE on our features reaches the level of the champion. A different model type can find more risk in the same features, but it can also be harder to explain. Thus the next question is: which type of model gives the score, and is the extra power worth the cost?

::: {#dec-04 .decision}
### Which type of model gives the score? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The model type sets how much risk the score finds. It also sets how easily the lender explains a decline, and how much work the model risk review needs. A model that is strong but that the lender cannot explain cannot go into production.

**Ways to do it.** We group all models for a yes/no target by how they make a decision. There are four groups, and each common model belongs to one of them. Each group then goes through three filters:

- **Predictive power on tabular data.** Our data is a table of numbers and categories, with missing values.
- **Explainability for the law.** The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) and Regulation B require the true reasons for each decline. The Federal Reserve guidance SR 11-7 requires that a reviewer can understand and test the model.
- **Deployment and control.** The model must give the same score in the decision system each day. The team must also check it each month.

| Group: how the model decides | Models | Predictive power | Explainability | Deployment | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance or geometry: an applicant is risky if it is near risky applicants or on the wrong side of a boundary | KNN, SVM | Medium. They need scaled numbers and no missing values. KNN is slow on `{python} N["n_train"]` loans. | Poor. "You are near five past defaults" is not a reason that a borrower can act on. | KNN keeps all training loans in the system. | Screened out |
| Connectionist: many layers of weights learn new features | Neural networks | Strong on images and text. On tables, usually not better than tree ensembles. | Poor. A black box. | More effort to fit and to monitor. | Screened out |
| Trees and rules: the model splits the applicants by rules | Decision tree, random forest, GBM | GBM: usually the best on tabular data. One tree: weak. Random forest: strong, but usually below the GBM. | Medium. Reason codes need a separate method, for example SHAP values. | Standard in risk systems. | Keep the GBM for the test |
| Parametric: one equation with one weight for each feature | Naive Bayes, logistic regression, logistic regression with WoE | Naive Bayes assumes that the features are independent. That is not true here (income and loan amount move together). Logistic regression: good. With WoE, it also captures curves and missing values. | Strong. Each WoE bin gives points. The reasons come directly from the points. | Simple: a table of points (a scorecard). | Keep logistic regression with WoE |

The shortlist has two models. The logistic regression with WoE is the industry scorecard: easy to explain, but it adds the effect of each feature without interactions. The GBM finds interactions, for example "short credit history and high card use", but it needs a separate method for reason codes.

The plan before the evidence: use the logistic regression with WoE, unless the GBM adds 2 KS points or more.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** Why WoE helps the logistic regression.

A plain logistic regression assumes that the log-odds change in a straight line with each raw value. It also cannot use a missing value. WoE first cuts each feature into ten bins on the training data, with a separate bin for missing values. It then replaces each value with the log-odds of its bin. Thus a curve in the raw value becomes a straight line in WoE, and a missing value gets its own risk.

The GBM uses the same features with the settings of `GBM_PARAMS`:

- learning rate 0.05 and at most 500 trees,
- at most 31 leaves for each tree and at least 200 loans in each leaf,
- an early stop on 10% of the training loans.
:::

**Evidence.** The code compares the champion and the two shortlisted models on the 2015 loans. Both models use the same features and the same training loans. The table gives branch 1 (AUC, Gini, KS) and branch 4. For branch 4, each model approves the most applicants at the champion bad rate. The last column gives the realized NPV of these approvals minus the realized NPV of the champion approvals.

```{python}
#| label: dec-04-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: champion, scorecard (logistic regression with WoE) and GBM"

# Purpose: Compare the scorecard (logistic regression with WoE) and the GBM with the champion (dec-04).
# Input:   `pd_test_lr`, `gbm_by_option`, `champ_rank`, `champ_ok`, `champ_bad`, `test['npv']`.
# Output:  `gbm` and `pd_test_gbm` (the benchmark), table `dec04`.

gbm, pd_test_gbm = gbm_by_option["B. Selection funnel"]  # The GBM of section 4a, on FEATURES
npv_all = test["npv"].to_numpy()


def gain_at_bad_rate(risk):
    """Return the approval share at the champion bad rate and its realized NPV against the champion ($M)."""
    share = approval_at_bad_rate(test["default"], risk, champ_bad)
    approved = np.argsort(risk, kind="stable")[: int(round(share * len(risk)))]
    return share, (npv_all[approved].sum() - npv_all[champ_ok].sum()) / 1e6


# Approval at the champion bad rate and its realized NPV: the business test of each score.
rows = [{"Model": "Champion: sub-grade only", **score_metrics(test["default"], champ_rank),
         "Approval at champion bad rate": champ_ok.mean(), "Realized NPV against champion ($M)": 0.0}]
for name, risk in [("Scorecard: logistic regression with WoE", pd_test_lr), ("GBM (benchmark)", pd_test_gbm)]:
    share, gain = gain_at_bad_rate(risk)
    rows.append({"Model": name, **score_metrics(test["default"], risk),
                 "Approval at champion bad rate": share, "Realized NPV against champion ($M)": gain})
dec04 = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Model")
dec04.insert(4, "Gain over champion (points)", (dec04["Approval at champion bad rate"] - champ_ok.mean()) * 100)

# The plan before the evidence: use the GBM only if it adds 2 KS points or more over the scorecard.
lr_row, gbm_row = dec04.iloc[1], dec04.iloc[2]
ks_gain = (gbm_row["KS"] - lr_row["KS"]) * 100
N.update({
    "lr_appr": f"{lr_row['Approval at champion bad rate']:.1%}",
    "gbm_appr": f"{gbm_row['Approval at champion bad rate']:.1%}",
    "lr_gain": f"{lr_row['Gain over champion (points)']:+.1f}",
    "gbm_gain": f"{gbm_row['Gain over champion (points)']:+.1f}",
    "ks_gain": f"{ks_gain:.1f}", "ks_vs_plan": "more than" if ks_gain >= 2 else "less than",
    "ks_lr": f"{lr_row['KS']:.3f}", "ks_gbm": f"{gbm_row['KS']:.3f}",
    "lr_npv_gain": money(lr_row["Realized NPV against champion ($M)"]),
    "gbm_npv_gain": money(gbm_row["Realized NPV against champion ($M)"]),
    "gbm_extra_appr": f"{gbm_row['Gain over champion (points)'] - lr_row['Gain over champion (points)']:.1f}",
    "gbm_extra_npv": money(gbm_row["Realized NPV against champion ($M)"] - lr_row["Realized NPV against champion ($M)"]),
})
fmt(dec04, {"AUC": "{:.3f}", "Gini": "{:.3f}", "KS": "{:.3f}", "Approval at champion bad rate": "{:.1%}",
            "Gain over champion (points)": "{:+.1f}", "Realized NPV against champion ($M)": "{:+,.1f}"})
```

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** The challenger is the scorecard: the logistic regression with WoE. The GBM stays as a benchmark. It shows the highest power that a black-box model gets from the same features. We keep the rule that we set before the evidence.
:::

**Why.** The GBM has a KS of `{python} N["ks_gbm"]`. The scorecard has `{python} N["ks_lr"]`. Thus the GBM adds only `{python} N["ks_gain"]` KS points, `{python} N["ks_vs_plan"]` the limit of 2 points in the plan. The evidence confirms the plan.

The business result agrees. At the champion bad rate of `{python} N["champ_bad"]`, the champion approves `{python} N["champ_appr"]` of applicants. The scorecard approves `{python} N["lr_appr"]` (`{python} N["lr_gain"]` points) and adds `{python} N["lr_npv_gain"]` of realized NPV on the 2015 loans. The GBM approves `{python} N["gbm_appr"]` (`{python} N["gbm_gain"]` points) and adds `{python} N["gbm_npv_gain"]`.

Thus the GBM gives `{python} N["gbm_extra_appr"]` more points of approval and `{python} N["gbm_extra_npv"]` more NPV than the scorecard. The lender accepts this smaller gain for three benefits:

- Each decline gets its reasons directly from the points of the scorecard (Step 5b).
- The model risk review is shorter, because a reviewer can read and test each weight.
- The scorecard is a table of points, so the decision system can apply it easily.

We set the rule of 2 KS points before we saw the evidence. A rule that changes after the evidence can follow the result that we want. Thus we keep the rule.

**What would change the decision.** Examine the GBM again in one of two conditions. A new vintage shows that the GBM adds 2 KS points or more. Or the business puts a higher value on the extra `{python} N["gbm_extra_npv"]` than on the cost of a longer model risk review.
:::

From here, the word "challenger" means the scorecard. The GBM appears again only as a benchmark. The next cell gives the challenger one name, so that Steps 5 to 7 do not depend on the model type.

```{python}
#| label: challenger
#| code-summary: "The challenger: the scorecard. The GBM stays as a benchmark."

# Purpose: Give the challenger one set of names for Steps 5 to 7 (dec-04).
# Input:   `m_lr`, `pd_test_lr`, `train`.
# Output:  `ch_name`, `ch_model`, `pd_test_ch` (PD on the 2015 loans), `pd_train_ch` (PD on the training loans).

ch_name = "Scorecard (logistic regression with WoE)"
ch_model = m_lr  # (WoE encoder, features, logistic regression)
pd_test_ch = pd_test_lr
pd_train_ch = pd_woe_lr(m_lr, train)
N["ch_name"] = ch_name
```

## 4d. Default rate: class imbalance and a change of level

The scorecard approves more applicants than the champion at the same bad rate. But Step 7 multiplies its PD by dollars to get the expected NPV. Thus the level of the PD must also be correct (branch 2). Two different problems can make the level wrong, and teams often mix them.

1. **Class imbalance.** Only about one loan in `{python} N["one_in"]` is a default (`{python} N["bad_train"]` in the training loans). Some teams then give more weight to the defaults, with a class weight or with synthetic defaults (SMOTE). These methods make the model behave as if defaults are more common than they are. Thus they push the PD up, far above the real default rate.
2. **A change of level over time.** The default rate went up from `{python} N["bad_train"]` in the training loans to `{python} N["bad_2015"]` in 2015 (Step 3b). A model that learns from 2013–2014 gives a PD at the level of 2013–2014.

The second problem is the more dangerous one, because it hides in the money. The chain is:

> Low default rate in training → PD too low for 2015 → expected NPV too high → a cutoff that approves loans with a negative NPV.

::: {#dec-05 .decision}
### How do we handle the default rate in the training data? {.unnumbered}

**Why this question matters.** The PD enters the expected NPV in dollars. A PD that is too high declines good applicants. A PD that is too low approves loans that lose money.

**Ways to do it.** The axis is where the correction happens: in the training data, in the model, or after the model. These three places cover all methods.

| Where | Method | Advantage | Main risk | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Training data | SMOTE (synthetic defaults) or fewer non-defaults | Balanced classes. | Synthetic rows. The PD becomes too high. Banks rarely use SMOTE for a PD model. | Screened out: the same effect as a class weight, with more risk |
| Model | Class weight: each default counts more in the fit | More weight to defaults. | The PD becomes too high. It needs a recalibration after the fit. | Test it |
| After the model | No change in the fit. Then move the level of the PD to the most recent default rate (recalibration). | The PD stays near the real rate. One constant to explain. | It needs recent loans with a known outcome. | Test it |

A default rate of `{python} N["bad_train"]` is not a rare event. Rare events, for example 1% or less, are a different case.

**Evidence.** The code trains the same scorecard again with a class weight, on the same WoE features. For each score decile of the 2015 loans, it compares the mean PD with the actual default rate (branch 2).

```{python}
#| label: dec-05-evidence
#| code-summary: "Evidence: calibration of the scorecard with and without a class weight"

# Purpose: Compare the calibration of the scorecard with and without a class weight (dec-05).
# Input:   `train`, `test`, `pd_test_ch`, `FEATURES`.
# Output:  Calibration chart and table `dec05`.

# The same scorecard with a class weight ("balanced": the defaults get the same total weight as the non-defaults).
m_lr_w = fit_woe_lr(train, FEATURES, class_weight="balanced")
pd_test_w = pd_woe_lr(m_lr_w, test)

# Mean PD and actual default rate for each score decile.
calib = pd.DataFrame({
    "decile": pd.qcut(pd_test_ch, 10, labels=False) + 1,
    "Actual": test["default"].to_numpy(),
    "No change": pd_test_ch,
    "Class weight": pd_test_w,
}).groupby("decile").mean()

N.update({"pd_mean": f"{pd_test_ch.mean():.1%}", "pd_mean_w": f"{pd_test_w.mean():.1%}",
          "bad_2015": f"{test['default'].mean():.1%}", "bad_train": f"{train['default'].mean():.1%}"})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
styles = {"Actual": (cs.GRAY, "o", "Actual"), "No change": (cs.NAVY, "s", "Scorecard"),
          "Class weight": (cs.BLUE, "^", "Scorecard, class weight")}
for col, (color, marker, label) in styles.items():
    ax.plot(calib.index, calib[col], marker=marker, color=color, lw=1.5 if col == "Actual" else 2)
    # "Actual" and "Scorecard" end near the same point. A vertical offset keeps the labels apart.
    dy = {"Actual": 6, "No change": -6, "Class weight": 0}[col]
    cs.label_end(ax, calib.index[-1], calib[col].iloc[-1], label, color=color, dy=dy, bold=(col == "Class weight"))
ax.set_xlabel("Score decile of the scorecard (1 = lowest risk)")
ax.set_ylabel("Default rate or mean PD")
ax.set_xticks(calib.index)
ax.set_xlim(0.5, 12.8)
cs.percent_axis(ax)
cs.action_title(fig, f"A class weight puts the mean PD at {pd_test_w.mean():.0%} against "
                     f"{test['default'].mean():.1%} actual",
                "Mean PD of the scorecard and actual default rate by score decile, 2015 loans")
plt.show()

dec05 = pd.DataFrame({
    "Option": ["No change", "Class weight"],
    "Mean predicted PD": [pd_test_ch.mean(), pd_test_w.mean()],
    "Actual default rate": [test["default"].mean()] * 2,
    "AUC": [roc_auc_score(test["default"], pd_test_ch), roc_auc_score(test["default"], pd_test_w)],
}).set_index("Option")
fmt(dec05, {"Mean predicted PD": "{:.1%}", "Actual default rate": "{:.1%}", "AUC": "{:.3f}"})
```

**How to read:** each point is one tenth of the 2015 loans, in order of the scorecard. The gray line is the actual default rate. The navy line is the scorecard without a change. The blue line is the scorecard with a class weight.

**So what:** the class weight keeps the order but puts the PD far too high. Without a change, the PD is close but a little too low in each decile.

::: {.choice}
**Decision.** No class weight and no SMOTE. In Step 5a, move the level of the PD to the default rate of the most recent loans (recalibration).
:::

**Why.** Both options give almost the same AUC, so they put applicants in almost the same order (branch 1). But the class weight gives a mean PD of `{python} N["pd_mean_w"]` against an actual default rate of `{python} N["bad_2015"]` (branch 2 fails). The expected NPV in Step 7 needs a correct PD.

Without a change, the mean PD is `{python} N["pd_mean"]`. This is the level of the training loans, not of 2015. The order is correct, but the level is too low. One constant on the log-odds scale corrects the level and keeps the order. Step 5a applies it.

**What would change the decision.** If the default rate is 1% or less, the model can miss the defaults. Then use a class weight and recalibrate after the fit.
:::

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The challenger is a scorecard on the application and credit bureau data, without the Lending Club sub-grade. At the champion bad rate, it approves `{python} N["lr_appr"]` of applicants against `{python} N["champ_appr"]` for the champion. The GBM approves `{python} N["gbm_appr"]`, but the lender keeps the scorecard for its clear reasons and its shorter review. The PD of the scorecard is too low for 2015, so Step 5 corrects the level and gives the reasons for each decline.
:::

# Step 5. Make predictions {#step-5}

::: {.bridge}
Step 4 selected the scorecard as the challenger, with the GBM as a benchmark. It left two open points. The PD of the scorecard is at the level of 2013–2014, too low for 2015. Each decline also needs its reasons in plain English. This step closes both points: what PD and what reasons does each 2015 applicant get?
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step gives each 2015 applicant a PD at the correct level and the reasons for a decline. It supports this decision: the score and the reason codes for the champion/challenger test.
:::

## 5a. Recalibration of the PD

Section 4d found that the mean PD of the scorecard is `{python} N["pd_mean"]`, but the 2015 loans default at `{python} N["bad_2015"]`. If we do not correct this, the expected NPV in Step 7 is too high, and the cutoff approves loans that lose money.

The correction uses one constant on the log-odds scale. The code adds the constant to the log-odds of each PD. The constant makes the mean PD equal to the default rate of the loans from January to June 2015. The loans from July to December 2015 then check the result. The recalibration does not change the order of the applicants. Thus the AUC, the KS and the swap-set do not change.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** PD after the recalibration = 1 / (1 + exp(−(ln(PD / (1 − PD)) + s))). The code finds the constant s with a root search (Brent's method) between −3 and 3. On the log-odds scale, one constant keeps the order of the applicants and keeps each PD between 0 and 1.

In production, the lender uses the most recent loans with a known outcome. An early sign of default, for example a payment 60 days late, can also help. Here the first half of 2015 has this role. The second half of 2015 is an honest check, because the constant never sees it.
:::

```{python}
#| label: recalibration
#| code-summary: "Recalibration: one constant on the log-odds scale, from the loans of January to June 2015"

# Purpose: Move the PD to the recent default rate with one constant on the log-odds scale (dec-05).
# Input:   `pd_test_ch` (PD of the scorecard), `test`, `y_test`, `logit()`, `expit()` (case01_helpers.py).
# Output:  `pd_cal` (the PD of the scorecard after the recalibration), `shift` (the constant), `h1`.

# Calibrate on January–June 2015. Check on July–December 2015.
h1 = (test["issue_date"].dt.month <= 6).to_numpy()
# Find the constant that makes the mean PD equal to the actual default rate.
shift = brentq(lambda s: expit(logit(pd_test_ch[h1]) + s).mean() - y_test[h1].mean(), -3, 3)
pd_cal = expit(logit(pd_test_ch) + shift)

N.update({"pd_h2_before": f"{pd_test_ch[~h1].mean():.1%}", "pd_h2_after": f"{pd_cal[~h1].mean():.1%}",
          "bad_h2": f"{y_test[~h1].mean():.1%}", "shift": f"{shift:+.3f}"})
fmt(pd.DataFrame({
    "Sample": ["January to June 2015 (calibration)", "July to December 2015 (check)"],
    "Actual default rate": [y_test[h1].mean(), y_test[~h1].mean()],
    "Mean PD before": [pd_test_ch[h1].mean(), pd_test_ch[~h1].mean()],
    "Mean PD after": [pd_cal[h1].mean(), pd_cal[~h1].mean()],
}).set_index("Sample"), {"Actual default rate": "{:.1%}", "Mean PD before": "{:.1%}",
                         "Mean PD after": "{:.1%}"})
```

The constant is `{python} N["shift"]` on the log-odds scale. On the check sample, the mean PD goes from `{python} N["pd_h2_before"]` before the recalibration to `{python} N["pd_h2_after"]` after it. The actual default rate is `{python} N["bad_h2"]`.

## 5b. Reason codes

A declined applicant must get the main reasons for the decline (ECOA and Regulation B). A scorecard gives the reasons directly from its points. This is the standard method for a scorecard, and model risk reviewers know it. It has three steps:

1. **Typical applicant.** Take the applicants that the scorecard approves at the champion approval rate. The typical value of each feature is the median for a number and the most common value for a category. The scorecard changes each typical value into its WoE.
2. **Points for each feature.** The points of a feature are its weight times a difference: the WoE of the applicant minus the WoE of the typical applicant. Positive points increase the log-odds of default, so they increase the PD.
3. **Reasons.** The three features with the most points are the reason codes. The table also gives the PD decrease if the feature takes the typical WoE.

::: {.tech-note}
**Technical note.** The scorecard gives log-odds of default = b₀ + Σ bⱼ × WoEⱼ. The points of feature j for an applicant are bⱼ × (WoEⱼ of the applicant − WoEⱼ of the typical approved applicant). The sum of the points is the difference in log-odds between the applicant and the typical applicant.

The PD goes up when the log-odds go up. Thus the order of the features by points is the same as the order by PD decrease. The reasons are exact for this model: no approximation, no sample and no random seed.
:::

A reason code is a column name, for example `bc_open_to_buy`. A borrower cannot read it. Thus each feature has a plain-English meaning in the dictionary `REASON_TEXT` (in `case01_helpers.py`). The direction tells if the value of the applicant is above or below the typical value. The direction then selects the text for the borrower, for example "Little unused credit on bank cards". If a feature is not in the dictionary, the column name becomes the text.

The table below gives the meaning of each feature of the challenger.

```{python}
#| label: reason-dictionary
#| code-summary: "Reason code dictionary: the plain-English meaning of each feature of the challenger"

# Purpose: Show the plain-English meaning of each feature that can become a reason code.
# Input:   `FEATURES`, `REASON_TEXT` (case01_helpers.py).
# Output:  Table: feature, meaning, text if the value is high, text if the value is low.

reason_dict = pd.DataFrame(
    [(c, *REASON_TEXT.get(c, (c, f"High value of {c}", f"Low value of {c}"))) for c in FEATURES],
    columns=["Feature", "Meaning", "Text if the value is high", "Text if the value is low"],
).set_index("Feature")
N["n_no_text"] = f"{sum(c not in REASON_TEXT for c in FEATURES)}"
reason_dict
```

```{python}
#| label: reason-codes
#| code-summary: "Reason codes: the three features with the most points, for one declined applicant"

# Purpose: Find the three features with the most points for one declined applicant of the scorecard.
# Input:   `ch_model`, `test`, `pd_test_ch`, `champ_ok`, `FEATURES`, `CAT_FEATURES`.
# Output:  `typical`, `woe_typ`, table of reason codes and the text for the borrower.

# The typical approved applicant: median of each number, most common category. Then its WoE.
ch_ok = approve_top(pd_test_ch, champ_ok.mean())
typical = test.loc[ch_ok, NUM_FEATURES].median()
for c in CAT_FEATURES:
    typical[c] = test.loc[ch_ok, c].mode().iloc[0]
woe_typ = typical_woe(ch_model, typical)

# One declined applicant: points and PD decrease of each feature.
example = test[~ch_ok].iloc[[0]]
pd_example = pd_woe_lr(ch_model, example)[0]
points = scorecard_points(ch_model, example, woe_typ).iloc[0]
effect = scorecard_reason_effects(ch_model, example, woe_typ).iloc[0]
top3 = points.sort_values(ascending=False).head(3)

rows = []
for c in top3.index:
    value, typ = example[c].iloc[0], typical[c]
    meaning, direction, text = describe_reason(c, value, typ, categorical=c in CAT_FEATURES)
    show = lambda v: v if isinstance(v, str) or pd.isna(v) else f"{v:,.4g}"  # Short text for a number
    rows.append({"Reason code": c, "Meaning": meaning, "Applicant value": show(value),
                 "Typical approved value": show(typ),
                 "Direction": direction, "Points (log-odds)": f"{top3[c]:+.3f}",
                 "PD decrease if typical": f"{effect[c]:.1%}", "Text for the borrower": text})
reasons = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=[1, 2, 3])

# The adverse action text: the three reasons in plain English.
notice = "; ".join(f"({i}) {t}" for i, t in zip(reasons.index, reasons["Text for the borrower"]))
N.update({"pd_example": f"{pd_example:.1%}", "notice": notice})
print(f"PD of the applicant after the recalibration: {expit(logit(pd_example) + shift):.1%}.")
print(f"Text for the borrower: We cannot approve your application now. The main reasons are: {notice}.")
reasons
```

**How to read:** each row is one reason, from the strongest. The "Meaning" column says what the feature measures. The "Points" column gives the increase of the log-odds of default. The "Text for the borrower" column is the sentence for the adverse action notice.

**So what:** the lender can send this text: "We cannot approve your application now. The main reasons are: `{python} N["notice"]`."

The points come from the weights of the model, not from an approximation. Thus a model risk reviewer can repeat each reason with a calculator.

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** Each 2015 applicant now has a PD at the 2015 level and, if declined, three reasons in plain English. Step 6 checks if the challenger passes all five branches of the evaluation framework.
:::

# Step 6. Evaluate {#step-6}

::: {.bridge}
Step 5 gave a PD at the correct level and reasons for each decline. Now we must judge the challenger as a whole. This step uses the five branches of the evaluation framework of Step 3a, one at a time. We keep the rules of Step 3a, also when a result is near a limit. If the challenger fails a branch, this step says why and what it means for the test.
:::

::: {.purpose}
**Purpose.** This step shows if the score is good enough for a test, in model metrics and in dollars. It supports this decision: approve the challenger score for the champion/challenger test.
:::

## 6a. Branch 1: order of risk

The question: does the challenger put risky applicants above safe applicants better than the champion? The rule of section 4c also applies: if the GBM benchmark is less than 2 KS points above the scorecard, the scorecard is enough. Section 3a gives the full rule. The table compares the scorecard with the champion and with the GBM on the 2015 loans. Section 3a explains the AUC, the Gini and the KS.

```{python}
#| label: eval-order
#| code-summary: "Branch 1: AUC, Gini and KS of the champion, the challenger (scorecard) and the GBM benchmark"

# Purpose: Measure branch 1 (order of risk) on the 2015 loans.
# Input:   `champ_rank`, `pd_cal`, `pd_test_gbm`, `y_test`.
# Output:  Table `eval_order`.

eval_order = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Score": "Champion: sub-grade", **score_metrics(y_test, champ_rank)},
    {"Score": "Challenger: scorecard after the recalibration", **score_metrics(y_test, pd_cal)},
    {"Score": "Benchmark: GBM", **score_metrics(y_test, pd_test_gbm)},
]).set_index("Score")
m_ch, m_champ = eval_order.iloc[1], eval_order.iloc[0]
N.update({"ks_ch": f"{m_ch['KS']:.3f}", "ks_champ": f"{m_champ['KS']:.3f}",
          "auc_ch": f"{m_ch['AUC']:.3f}", "auc_champ6": f"{m_champ['AUC']:.3f}",
          "gini_ch": f"{m_ch['Gini']:.3f}", "gini_champ": f"{m_champ['Gini']:.3f}"})
fmt(eval_order, {"AUC": "{:.3f}", "Gini": "{:.3f}", "KS": "{:.3f}"})
```

The challenger has an AUC of `{python} N["auc_ch"]` against `{python} N["auc_champ6"]` for the champion, and a Gini of `{python} N["gini_ch"]` against `{python} N["gini_champ"]`. The gain is small. On the KS, the two scores are almost equal: `{python} N["ks_ch"]` against `{python} N["ks_champ"]`.

The rule of branch 1 is a KS above the champion. The scorecard does not pass it: on the whole population, it ranks risk about as well as the sub-grades. We do not change the rule after the evidence. The value of the scorecard is in a smaller region: the applicants near the cutoff. Branch 4 measures this region directly.

The GBM benchmark is `{python} N["ks_gain"]` KS points above the scorecard, less than the limit of 2 points. The recalibration does not change the AUC or the KS of the scorecard.

## 6b. Branch 2: level

The question: does the mean PD match the actual default rate, on loans that the recalibration did not use? The check uses the loans of July to December 2015. The chart compares the PD before and after the recalibration with the actual default rate, for each score decile.

```{python}
#| label: eval-level
#| code-summary: "Branch 2: mean PD against the actual default rate, July to December 2015"

# Purpose: Measure branch 2 (level) on the check sample (July–December 2015).
# Input:   `pd_test_ch`, `pd_cal`, `y_test`, `h1`.
# Output:  Calibration chart. `level_gap` (mean PD after the recalibration minus the actual rate).

chk = ~h1
level = pd.DataFrame({
    "decile": pd.qcut(pd_cal[chk], 10, labels=False) + 1,
    "Actual": y_test[chk], "Before": pd_test_ch[chk], "After": pd_cal[chk],
}).groupby("decile").mean()
level_gap = pd_cal[chk].mean() - y_test[chk].mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for col, color, marker in [("Actual", cs.GRAY, "o"), ("Before", cs.LIGHT_GRAY, "s"), ("After", cs.NAVY, "^")]:
    ax.plot(level.index, level[col], marker=marker, color=color, lw=2 if col == "After" else 1.5)
    label = {"Actual": "Actual", "Before": "Scorecard, before", "After": "Scorecard, after"}[col]
    # The three lines end near the same point. A vertical offset keeps the labels apart.
    dy = {"Actual": 10, "Before": -10, "After": 0}[col]
    cs.label_end(ax, level.index[-1], level[col].iloc[-1], label, color=color, dy=dy, bold=(col == "After"))
ax.set_xlabel("Score decile of the scorecard (1 = lowest risk)")
ax.set_ylabel("Default rate or mean PD")
ax.set_xticks(level.index)
ax.set_xlim(0.5, 12.3)
cs.percent_axis(ax)
cs.action_title(fig, f"After the recalibration, the mean PD is {pd_cal[chk].mean():.1%} "
                     f"against {y_test[chk].mean():.1%} actual",
                "Mean PD and actual default rate by score decile, loans of July to December 2015")
plt.show()
```

**How to read:** each point is one tenth of the check loans, in order of the scorecard. The gray line is the actual default rate. The light gray line is the PD of the scorecard before the recalibration, and the navy line is the PD after it.

**So what:** after the recalibration, the PD follows the actual default rate. The expected NPV in Step 7 can use it.

## 6c. Branch 3: stability

The question: do the 2015 applicants look like the training applicants? If not, the score can lose power soon after the start of the test. The code calculates the PSI of the challenger score from the training loans to the 2015 loans. Rule 11 of section 4a already removed each feature with a PSI of more than 0.1. The table repeats the largest PSI of the final features.

```{python}
#| label: eval-stability
#| code-summary: "Branch 3: PSI of the score and of the features, training loans against 2015 loans"

# Purpose: Measure branch 3 (stability): PSI of the score and of each feature.
# Input:   `pd_train_ch`, `pd_cal`, `shift`, `psi_col` (section 4a), `FEATURES`.
# Output:  `psi_score`, table of the PSI.

# PD of the training loans, with the same recalibration, for the PSI.
psi_score = psi(expit(logit(pd_train_ch) + shift), pd_cal)
psi_feat = psi_col.reindex(FEATURES).dropna()
N.update({"psi_score": f"{psi_score:.3f}", "psi_feat_max": f"{psi_feat.max():.3f}",
          "psi_feat_top": psi_feat.idxmax()})
fmt(pd.DataFrame({
    "PSI": [psi_score, psi_feat.max(), psi_feat.median()],
    "Rule": ["Less than 0.1"] * 3,
}, index=["Challenger score", f"Largest feature PSI ({psi_feat.idxmax()})", "Median feature PSI"]),
    {"PSI": "{:.3f}"})
```

The PSI of the score is `{python} N["psi_score"]`. The largest feature PSI is `{python} N["psi_feat_max"]` (`{python} N["psi_feat_top"]`). Both are less than 0.1, so the population is stable. Section 3b showed that the level of the default rate changed. The recalibration in Step 5a corrects that change.

## 6d. Branch 4: business value

The question: at the same risk, does the challenger approve more applicants and add NPV? Two tests answer it.

- **Approval at the champion bad rate.** How many applicants can the challenger approve, at the bad rate of the champion?
- **Swap-set.** At the same number of approvals, which loans does the challenger change, and are the new loans better?

```{python}
#| label: eval-approval
#| code-summary: "Branch 4: approval at the champion bad rate"

# Purpose: Measure the approval of the challenger at the champion bad rate.
# Input:   `pd_cal`, `y_test`, `champ_bad`, `champ_ok`.
# Output:  `appr_ch` (approval share of the challenger).

appr_ch = approval_at_bad_rate(y_test, pd_cal, champ_bad)
N.update({"appr_ch": f"{appr_ch:.1%}", "appr_gain": f"{(appr_ch - champ_ok.mean()) * 100:+.1f}"})
print(f"At the champion bad rate of {champ_bad:.1%}: the champion approves {champ_ok.mean():.1%}, "
      f"the challenger approves {appr_ch:.1%}.")
```

At the champion bad rate, the challenger approves `{python} N["appr_ch"]` of applicants, against `{python} N["champ_appr"]` for the champion (`{python} N["appr_gain"]` points).

**How the swap-set works.** The test gives both policies the same number of approvals: the champion approval share of `{python} N["champ_appr"]`. Each 2015 applicant then falls into one of four groups:

| Group | Champion | Challenger | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Both approve | Approve | Approve | No change. |
| Swap-in | Decline | Approve | New approvals of the challenger. |
| Swap-out | Approve | Decline | New declines of the challenger. |
| Both decline | Decline | Decline | No change. |

Both policies approve the same number of applicants. Thus the swap-in group and the swap-out group have the same size. Only these two groups change the result.

The champion declines the sub-grades `{python} N["champ_cut_sg"]` and worse. Lending Club booked all these loans, so we know the real outcome of each swap-in loan. This is a form of reject inference with real outcomes. The limit: the data has no applicant that Lending Club declined. Step 7 examines this limit.

```{python}
#| label: swap-set
#| code-summary: "Swap-set at the approval rate of the champion (2015 loans)"

# Purpose: Compare the champion and the challenger at the same approval rate (swap-set).
# Input:   `pd_cal`, `champ_ok`, `test`, `y_test`.
# Output:  Table `swap` with four groups. `npv_test` (realized NPV of each 2015 loan), `chall_ok`.

npv_test = test["npv"].to_numpy()
# The challenger approves the same number of applicants as the champion.
chall_ok = approve_top(pd_cal, champ_ok.mean())
# Four groups. The swap-in and swap-out groups have the same size.
groups = {
    "Both approve": champ_ok & chall_ok,
    "Swap-in (challenger approves, champion declines)": chall_ok & ~champ_ok,
    "Swap-out (champion approves, challenger declines)": champ_ok & ~chall_ok,
    "Both decline": ~champ_ok & ~chall_ok,
}
swap = pd.DataFrame([{
    "Group": name, "Loans": m.sum(), "Default rate": y_test[m].mean(),
    "Interest rate": test["int_rate"].to_numpy()[m].mean() / 100,
    "Realized NPV for each loan": npv_test[m].mean(),
    "Total realized NPV ($M)": npv_test[m].sum() / 1e6,
} for name, m in groups.items()]).set_index("Group")

s_in, s_out = swap.iloc[1], swap.iloc[2]
swap_gain = s_in["Total realized NPV ($M)"] - s_out["Total realized NPV ($M)"]
N.update({
    "swap_n": f"{s_in['Loans']:,.0f}", "swap_share": f"{s_in['Loans'] / len(test):.1%}",
    "swap_in_bad": f"{s_in['Default rate']:.1%}", "swap_out_bad": f"{s_out['Default rate']:.1%}",
    "swap_in_rate": f"{s_in['Interest rate']:.1%}", "swap_out_rate": f"{s_out['Interest rate']:.1%}",
    "swap_gain": money(swap_gain),
})
fmt(swap, {"Loans": "{:,.0f}", "Default rate": "{:.1%}", "Interest rate": "{:.1%}",
           "Realized NPV for each loan": lambda v: money(v, "", 0), "Total realized NPV ($M)": "{:,.1f}"})
```

The two policies do not agree on `{python} N["swap_n"]` loans in each group (`{python} N["swap_share"]` of the 2015 loans). The swap-in loans have a default rate of `{python} N["swap_in_bad"]`. The swap-out loans have a default rate of `{python} N["swap_out_bad"]`. With the same number of approvals, the challenger adds `{python} N["swap_gain"]` of realized NPV.

The swap-in loans also have a higher interest rate (`{python} N["swap_in_rate"]` against `{python} N["swap_out_rate"]`). The challenger finds applicants in lower grades with less risk than their grade shows. Lending Club gave these applicants a high interest rate.

The champion is an assumption (as-04). The table below repeats the approval test for three champion approval rates: 80%, 85% and 90%. For each one, the challenger must reach the bad rate of that champion.

```{python}
#| label: champion-sensitivity
#| code-summary: "Sensitivity: approval gain for three champion approval rates"

# Purpose: Repeat the approval gain for three champion approval rates (as-04).
# Input:   `champ_rank`, `pd_cal`, `y_test`.
# Output:  Table `sens` of the gain for each champion.

rows = []
# For each champion: its bad rate, then the challenger approval at that bad rate.
for share in (0.80, 0.85, 0.90):
    cut = np.sort(champ_rank)[int(share * len(champ_rank))]
    ok = champ_rank < cut
    bad = y_test[ok].mean()
    rows.append({"Champion approval target": share, "Champion approval": ok.mean(),
                 "Champion bad rate": bad,
                 "Challenger approval at the same bad rate": approval_at_bad_rate(y_test, pd_cal, bad)})
sens = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Champion approval target")
sens["Gain (points)"] = (sens["Challenger approval at the same bad rate"] - sens["Champion approval"]) * 100
sens.index = [f"{s:.0%}" for s in sens.index]
N["sens_min_gain"] = f"{sens['Gain (points)'].min():+.1f}"
fmt(sens, {"Champion approval": "{:.1%}", "Champion bad rate": "{:.1%}",
           "Challenger approval at the same bad rate": "{:.1%}", "Gain (points)": "{:+.1f}"})
```

The smallest gain of the three champions is `{python} N["sens_min_gain"]` points. Thus the result does not depend on the exact champion assumption.

## 6e. Branch 5: explainability

The question: can the lender give true reasons for each decline, not only for the example of Step 5b? The code repeats the points method on a random sample of 1,000 declined applicants. For each applicant, it counts the features with positive points. It also checks that each of the three reasons has a plain-English text.

```{python}
#| label: eval-reasons
#| code-summary: "Branch 5: reason codes for a sample of 1,000 declined applicants"

# Purpose: Measure branch 5: do the declined applicants get three reasons with a plain-English text?
# Input:   `ch_model`, `test`, `chall_ok`, `woe_typ`, `REASON_TEXT`.
# Output:  `reason_ok` (share with three valid reasons), table of the most common first reasons.

# A random sample of 1,000 declined applicants (fixed seed).
declined = test[~chall_ok].sample(1000, random_state=SEED)
eff = scorecard_points(ch_model, declined, woe_typ)
# For each applicant: the three strongest reasons. A valid reason increases the PD and has a text.
top = eff.apply(lambda r: list(r.sort_values(ascending=False).index[:3]), axis=1)
n_up = (eff > 0).sum(axis=1)
has_text = top.apply(lambda cols: all(c in REASON_TEXT for c in cols))
reason_ok = ((n_up >= 3) & has_text).mean()
N.update({"reason_ok": f"{reason_ok:.0%}"})

# The most common first reason in the sample.
first = top.str[0].value_counts(normalize=True).head(5)
N["first_reasons"] = ", ".join(REASON_TEXT.get(c, (c,))[0].lower() for c in first.index[:3])
fmt(pd.DataFrame({"Meaning": [REASON_TEXT.get(c, (c,))[0] for c in first.index],
                  "Share of declines": first.to_numpy()}, index=first.index.rename("First reason")),
    {"Share of declines": "{:.0%}"})
```

`{python} N["reason_ok"]` of the sampled declines have three reasons with positive points, each with a plain-English text. The table shows the most common first reasons. The three most common are: `{python} N["first_reasons"]`. A credit officer can check that each one makes sense for a decline.

## 6f. Summary of the evaluation

The table collects one result for each branch.

```{python}
#| label: evaluate
#| code-summary: "Summary: the challenger against the rule of each branch"

# Purpose: Collect the result of the challenger for each branch of the evaluation framework.
# Input:   Results of sections 6a–6e, `ks_gain` (section 4c).
# Output:  Table `evaluation`.

evaluation = pd.DataFrame([
    ("1. Order of risk", "KS: challenger / champion; KS of the GBM benchmark minus the challenger",
     f"{m_ch['KS']:.3f} / {m_champ['KS']:.3f}; {ks_gain:+.1f} points",
     "KS above the champion; GBM less than 2 KS points above (the scorecard is enough)",
     round(m_ch["KS"], 3) > round(m_champ["KS"], 3) and ks_gain < 2),
    ("2. Level", "Mean PD minus actual rate, July–December 2015", f"{level_gap * 100:+.1f} points",
     "Less than 1 point", abs(level_gap) < 0.01),
    ("3. Stability", "PSI of the score; largest feature PSI", f"{psi_score:.3f}; {psi_feat.max():.3f}",
     "Less than 0.1", psi_score < 0.1 and psi_feat.max() < 0.1),
    ("4. Business value", "Approval at the champion bad rate; swap-set NPV",
     f"{appr_ch:.1%} against {champ_ok.mean():.1%}; {swap_gain:+.1f} $M",
     "More approvals and a positive NPV", appr_ch > champ_ok.mean() and swap_gain > 0),
    ("5. Explainability", "Declines with three reasons in plain English", f"{reason_ok:.0%}",
     "95% or more", reason_ok >= 0.95),
], columns=["Branch", "Metric", "Result", "Rule", "Pass"]).set_index("Branch")
evaluation["Pass"] = evaluation["Pass"].map({True: "Yes", False: "No"})
N["n_pass"] = f"{(evaluation['Pass'] == 'Yes').sum()}"
evaluation
```

::: {.business-note}
**Business note.** The challenger passes `{python} N["n_pass"]` of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. It does not rank risk better than the sub-grades on the whole population (branch 1). But it orders the applicants near the cutoff better, and that is where the approval decision happens.

With the same number of approvals as the champion, it replaces `{python} N["swap_n"]` loans. The new loans default less (`{python} N["swap_in_bad"]` against `{python} N["swap_out_bad"]`) and add `{python} N["swap_gain"]` of realized NPV on the 2015 loans. Step 7 changes the score into a cutoff and a test plan.
:::

# Step 7. Implementation {#step-7}

::: {.bridge}
Step 6 showed that the challenger, the scorecard, passes `{python} N["n_pass"]` of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. It ranks the whole population about as well as the sub-grades, but it orders the applicants near the cutoff better. At the same number of approvals, it swaps `{python} N["swap_n"]` loans and adds `{python} N["swap_gain"]` of realized NPV. A better order is not yet a policy. This step answers the last question: where do we put the cutoff, how much is it worth, and how do we test it safely?

**Purpose.** This step changes the score into an approval rule, a dollar value and a test plan. It supports this decision: the cutoff for the champion/challenger test, and go or no-go.
